On 8 and 9 November 2012, the Secretariat informed the parties that the Commission considered the Communication at its 52 Ordinary Session held from 9 to 22 October 2012 in Yamoussoukro, Côte d'Ivoire, and that a decision will be taken based on the information in its possession.

On 10 May 2013, the Secretariat informed the parties that the Commission considered the Communication during its 53 Ordinary Session held from 9 to 23 April 2013 in Banjul, The Gambia, and decided to defer its decision on admissibility to its next Session. The Commission decided once again to defer the admissibility decision to its 54 Ordinary Session. The parties were duly informed of this decision.

At its 15 Extraordinary Session held from 7 to 14 March 2014 in Banjul, The Gambia, the Commission gave a decision on admissibility. The parties were informed accordingly on 17 March 2014 and on the same date the Complainants were requested to submit on the merits.

On 3 May 2014, the Complainants requested the Commission for additional time and requested for the beneficiaries and additional victims to join the suit. On 6 May 2014, the Commission granted an additional period of thirty (30) days and indicated that the joinder request will be considered by the Commission at the merits stage.

On 26 June 2014, the Secretariat received the Complainants' observations on the merits. The Secretariat forwarded the same to the Respondent State on 8 July 2014 and wrote to the Complainants acknowledging receipt.

At its 17 Extraordinary Session held from 19 to 28 February 2015 in Banjul, The Gambia, the Commission decided that before striking out a case or delivering a default judgment, it would consistently send reminders and grant a final deadline of thirty (30) days to parties that have not submitted their observations within the period prescribed under the Rules of Procedure. On 6 March 2015, such a letter was sent to the Respondent State concerning this Communication but there was no reaction. At its successive sessions, the Commission considered the Communication and deferred the same due to time constraints.

The Complainants submit that the Communication meets the conditions under Article 56 of the African Charter. They elaborate on the conditions under Article 56 (4), (5) and (6). With regard to Article 56(4), they submit that the Communication is based on information gathered during a field mission to the DRC from 17 April to 1 May 2010 and from other reliable sources.

Regarding the conditions under the two other paragraphs of Article 56, the Complainants first of all present arguments on the admissibility of the cases of Ulimwengu Lukumani, Ulimwengu Nombele and the Ulimwengu family; cases that were brought before the Congolese courts. They then elaborate on the cases of Kunda Musopelo Pierre, the Kunda family, of X and Y that were not brought before the Congolese courts.

Regarding the first three cases, the Complainants assert that the condition of the exhaustion of local remedies under Article 56(5) has been met. Thus, the Complainants contend that the Katanga Military Court was seized of the referral decision of 12 October 2006 by the Military Prosecutor in respect of the case involving war crimes and crimes against humanity committed by Colonel Adémar and eight (8) members of the FARDC, and passed its judgement No. 010/2006 on 28 June 2007 acquitting all the accused persons for lack of evidence.

The Complainants assert that the appeal lodged against this judgement before the Military High Court by the parties to the Kilwa suit was declared inadmissible for lack of special powers of attorney regarding the civil parties (Complainants) whereas the lawyers were the same who represented the Complainants before the Military Court. The Complainants further allege that the general appeal filed by Major Ndaka, Deputy Military Prosecutor, was also dismissed on the grounds that he was not of the same rank as Colonel Ilunga Adémar, the main defendant. The Complainants allege that given that the Military High Court is the highest court of appeal in the matter, it means local remedies have been exhausted.

Regarding the cases of Kunda Musopelo Pierre, the Kunda family, of X and Y, the Complainants acknowledge that the victims did not refer the matter to the Congolese judicial authorities. They justify this situation by stating that given the above-mentioned cases, the courts were partial because the responsibility of the perpetrators of violations was not established by the Congolese military courts, in spite of the testimonies of victims and the existence of mass graves.

The Complainants assert that the Military High Court's decision is tangible proof of the lack of objectivity on the part of the courts concerned with regard to the human rights violations that were committed in Kilwa in October 2004. Citing from jurisprudential sources, Jawara v. The Gambia, the Complainants aver that the local remedies offered to Kunda Musopelo Pierre and to X and Y were ineffective, and pray the Commission to consider that local remedies were exhausted.

Still on the issue of exhaustion of local remedies, the Complainants further aver that the involvement of members of the armed forces in the violations suffered by Pierre Kunda Musopelo, X and Y, is not likely to encourage the quest for justice in the DRC. In this regard, they mention Communication No. 1186/2003 in which, in order to declare a Communication against Cameroon admissible, the UN Human Rights Committee stated that the involvement of the Executive and the military of the Republic of Cameroon in human rights violations rendered local remedies ineffective. In this regard, they contend that it would not only be risky for the victims to refer the matter to the Congolese courts, but also that such an action would have no prospect of success.

Regarding the condition on submitting the Communication within a reasonable period after exhausting local remedies as provided under Article 56(6) of the African Charter, the Complainants assert that even though the period of six months which is generally applied by the Commission in its jurisprudence was not respected, there is corroborating evidence to justify an exception to this rule.

As such, the Complainants submit that despite the efforts made by the parties to the suit, they were still not notified about the Military High Court's decision at the time the matter was brought before the Commission. The Complainants further assert that it is difficult, and even impossible, to take any other legal action in the DRC given that they were never informed of the grounds on which the Military High Court made its decision.

The Complainants are of the view that the serious and massive nature of the violations (73 people reported to have been summarily executed during the events in Kilwa) should prompt the Commission to be indulgent in its consideration of the condition of reasonable period. The Complainants assert that such an approach will help to provide justice to dozens of victims whose complaints were not considered on the merits by the Congolese Military High Court.

Lastly, regarding reasonable period, the Complainants raise the issue of the inaccessibility of the Kilwa region as one of the reasons justifying the three years that elapsed between the time local remedies were exhausted and the time the matter was brought before the Commission. They assert that Kilwa is 350 km north of Lubumbashi where the courts are found and that the road to Kilwa gets very bad during the rainy season, so much so that travelling from Kilwa to Lubumbashi can easily take a week. Thus, they contend that the inaccessibility of Kilwa not only makes it difficult to have access to judicial institutions, but also difficult for the victims to enjoy legal assistance under acceptable conditions.
The Respondent State did not submit any observations on admissibility in spite of several requests from the Secretariat.

The Communication was submitted in accordance with Article 55 of the African Charter which mandates the Commission to receive and consider "Communications other than those of State Parties". For a Communication to be declared admissible, it has to meet the conditions laid down in Article 56 of the African Charter.

In accordance with the Rules of Procedure of the Commission, when the latter is seized of a Communication, it promptly informs the parties and requests the Complainant to present evidence and arguments on admissibility within two months. Upon receipt of the Complainant's observations, the Secretariat transmits a copy to the Respondent State and requests the latter to submit its observations within two months of its receipt of the Commission's request.

In this Communication, the Commission notes that the abovementioned procedure was followed, and that the Respondent State did not submit any observations on admissibility despite the various reminders. As such, the Commission decides to consider the Communication on the basis of the information in its possession.

In examining the conditions of admissibility under Article 56 of the African Charter, the Commission will dwell on the conditions that the Complainants claim to have unequivocally been met before examining the conditions under Article 56 (5) and (6). Regarding the latter conditions, the Complainants provide more substantial arguments.

Article 56(1) stipulates that Communications should indicate their authors even if the latter request anonymity. In this Communication, the identities of the authors are clearly stated. The authors are the Institute for Human Rights and Development in Africa, Action against Impunity for Human Rights, and Rights and Accountability in Development, representing Kunda Musopelo Pierre, the Kunda family, Ulimwengu Lukumani, Ulimwengu Nombele, the Ulimwengu family, as well as X and Y who requested anonymity. The Commission concludes that this condition has been met.

Regarding Article 56(2) which stipulates that Communications must be compatible with the Charter of the Organisation of African Unity or with the African Charter, the Commission notes that the Communication reveals a prima facie violation by a State Party of human rights guaranteed by the African Charter, in particular the rights laid down in Articles 1, 4, 5, 6, 7(1), 14 and 26 of the Charter. The Commission concludes that the condition under Article 56(2) has been met.

Article 56(3) stipulates that Communications must not be written in disparaging or insulting language directed against the State concerned and its institutions or to the OAU/AU. Considering the Complaint, the Commission considers that the Complainants have not used any such language. It follows that this condition has been met.

Under Article 56(4), Communications must not be based exclusively on news disseminated through the mass media. The Commission notes that the information provided by the Complainants is mostly based on the findings of a field mission during which they gathered testimonies of victims. As such, the Commission concludes that this condition has been met.

Regarding Article 56(7), the Commission refers to the facts provided by the Complainants and notes that the Communication does not deal with a case which has been settled in accordance with the principles of the Charter of the United Nations, or the Constitutive Act of the African Union or the provisions of the African Charter. The Commission thus concludes that the condition under Article 56(7) has been met.

Article 56(5) of the African Charter stipulates that Communications must be submitted after exhausting local remedies, if any, unless it is obvious to the Commission that this procedure is unduly prolonged. The objective of this principle of international law is to prevent international bodies from playing the role of courts of first instance. It is also to enable the Respondent State to take cognizance of the charges brought against it and to redress them, if necessary, through its legal system.

In its jurisprudence regarding its interpretation of Article 56(5), the Commission decided in the case of Jawara v. The Gambia that remedies to be exhausted must be available, effective and sufficient. As such, the Commission decided that: A remedy is considered available if the petitioner can pursue it without impediment, it is deemed effective if it offers a prospect of success, and it is found sufficient if it is capable of redressing the complaint.

In this Communication, the Complainants aver that local remedies were exhausted in the case of the first three victims. In the case of the other four victims, they assert that the matter was not brought before the local courts, arguing that there was tacit exhaustion of local remedies given that such remedies would have produced the same results. For reasons of clarity, the Commission will examine the two cases separately as presented by the Complainants.

Regarding the victims Ulimwengu Lukumani, Ulimwengu Nombele and the Ulimwengu family, the Commission notes that under Congolese Law No. 023/2002 of 18 November 2002 on the Military Judicial Code, the courts seized by the victims were courts which have jurisdiction over the crimes alleged to have been committed. Besides, the Commission notes that in accordance with Section 83 of the same law, the Military High Court handles appeals against the decisions of military trial courts of first instance and its decisions are final.

The Commission further notes that on 28 June 2007, the Katanga Military Court ruled on the accusations brought against the alleged perpetrators of the crimes committed. On December 21 of the same year, the Military High Court dismissed the appeal against this ruling even though, at the time the Commission was seized of the matter, the Complainants had not been notified of the dismissal ruling.

In any case, the Commission notes that the dismissal ruling, which did not favour the Complainants, put an end to local remedies given that there is no higher court that can deal with the case. Even if an appeal were possible, the lack of notification made such an avenue impossible. The Commission concludes that local remedies should be considered as having been exhausted regarding the victims concerned.

With regard to the case of Kunda Musopelo Pierre, the Kunda family, X and Y, the Complainants submit that these victims did not seize the local courts as a result of the partiality with which the courts handled the case filed by the first group of complainants, given that such remedies would not have been effective. The Complainants further submit that the involvement of members of the armed forces in the violations suffered by Kunda Musopelo Pierre, X and Y is not likely to enhance the pursuit of justice in the DRC. In other words, the Complainants doubt the prospect of success of local remedies.

On this issue, the Commission reiterates that it is incumbent on the Complainant as a minimum obligation to attempt to exhaust local remedies and not to make efforts to exhaust obviously ineffective remedies. In this regard, the Commission notes that in the present Communication, the situation complained about by all the victims is characterised by similar factual and legal factors.

Thus, the alleged violations were committed under the same circumstances in terms of time, 15 October 2004, in the same place (Kilwa) and by the same people (the FARDC). These factual elements, considered by the local courts and based on which their decision was made, are the same for the two categories of victims. Besides, and in view of the above, even if the victims of the second group decided to seek local remedies, their case would have been heard by the same courts.

In the light of these findings, it is difficult not to form an opinion that bringing the matter before these courts would have led to an identical or similar outcome. It can be concluded that such remedies did not offer any prospect of success and that the condition for their success was not met. Under such circumstances, local remedies should be considered to have been exhausted. As such, the Commission concludes that regarding the second group of victims, the Communication meets the condition under Article 56(5) of the African Charter.

Furthermore, the Commission will determine if, as stipulated in Article 56(6) of the African Charter, the Communication was submitted within a reasonable period from the time local remedies were exhausted or from the date the Commission was seized of the matter.

Even though the African Charter does not clearly define the notion of "reasonable period" within which a Complaint should be submitted after exhausting local remedies, the Commission, drawing from the practice of the Inter-American and European systems, decided in the case of Majuru v. Zimbabwe that a period of six months can be considered as a "standard requirement".

Moreover, the Commission has stated in its jurisprudence that "reasonable period" within which a Communication should be submitted should be decided on a case-by-case basis while taking into account the circumstances of the case. As such, in the case of Chinhamo v. Zimbabwe, the Commission decided that given the exceptional circumstances in which the Complainant found himself – living in exile, ten months was a reasonable period for him to submit his complaint.

In the light of the jurisprudence recalled in this context, the issue the Commission needs to resolve in this case is whether the period within which the Commission was seized of this Communication can be viewed as reasonable. In this regard, the Commission notes that close to three years elapsed between the time local remedies were exhausted and the date it was seized of the Complaint. In order to justify that this period of time is reasonable, the Complainants attribute the delay to the physical inaccessibility of the courts and the lack of notification by the Military High Court of its judgement. They also raise the issue of perpetration of serious and massive violations.

On the issue of inaccessibility of the courts, the Commission notes that the distance between the Complainants' place of residence and the location of the courts in Kilwa is 350 km. Considering this factor, it would be unlikely that three years elapsed in covering such a distance even under the most difficult conditions. As the Complainants themselves assert, travelling to Kilwa under such conditions could easily take a week. Moreover, the Commission therefore concludes that even though it may have played a part in this, the poor state of the road alone cannot justify the delay in the seizure cited above.

Regarding the lack of notification of the Military High Court's judgement, the Commission agrees that such a situation is likely to delay its seizure by the Complainant. Indeed, the said Court is the highest court of appeal and its judgement gives rise to exhaustion of local remedies. Incidentally, the lack of notification could leave the Complainants in doubt concerning not only the issue of procedure but also the grounds for the judgement delivered. In this case, it is material impediment.

Moreover, besides the material impossibility which it took into account in the Chinhano case cited supra, one of the factors frequently used by the Commission to determine reasonable period is the need to ensure fairness and justice. The Commission used this factor as grounds for its decision in the case of Darfur Relief and Documentation Centre v. Sudan. The Commission at that time decided that though the objective of Article 56(6) is to discourage any delay in seizure, it is also incumbent upon it to provide an opportunity for the Complainant to be heard when valid and appropriate reasons have accounted for such a delay. The relevant factor in these circumstances is the "need for fairness and justice". The Commission is of the view that such a factor is crucial in specific situations where local remedies did not meet the need for fairness and justice which must be the objective of any procedure aimed at protecting human rights guaranteed by the African Charter.

The Commission is therefore of the view that the "need for fairness and justice" is motivated by a more determining reason which is to ensure that the Commission is in a position to consider the Communication in an appropriate and fair manner. The related issue is whether in the circumstances of this case, the time element for the seizure of the Commission played a role in rendering the evidence inaccessible or changed them to the extent that an appropriate consideration was made extremely difficult or impossible. The decisive reason in such situations is therefore one of "fair consideration" of the case.

In the present case, and as highlighted above, the Complainants raise the issue of non-compliance with certain minimum rules of a fair trial, and the partiality and ineffectiveness of local procedures coupled with the lack of notification of the decision of the highest competent court. Under such circumstances, the Commission is of the view that failure to declare the Communication admissible will deprive the victims of fairness and justice which they had already been deprived of at the national level.

On the issue of the need for a fair review of the Communication, the Commission is of the view that looking at the different elements presented by the Complainants, the case needs to be considered on its merits. In fact, the initial Complaint and the subsequent submissions contain sufficient information to provide the Complainants with the opportunity to be heard on the merits. In addition, looking at the number of summary executions reported, this Communication obviously concerns a case of massive human rights violations. In the view of the Commission, the massive nature of the violations highlights the need to guarantee the principles outlined above and consequently consider the merits to avoid any risk of denial of justice in a case involving such serious allegations.

In these circumstances, the Commission finds that the timeframe for the Complainants to seize the Commission is not unreasonable. The Commission therefore concludes that the Communication meets the condition under Article 56 (6) of the African Charter.
In view of the foregoing, the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights declares the Communication admissible in accordance with Article 56 of the African Charter.

Even though the Complaint was initially filed on behalf of Kunda Musopelo Pierre, the Kunda family, Ulimwengu Lukumani, Ulimwengu Nombele, the Ulimwengu family, as well as X and Y; the Complainants submitted at the merits stage a request for joinder for the victims AAA, CCC, LLL, MMM and Mpweto Malangisha Pélagie who are either beneficiaries or deceased.

The Complainants recall the Commission's jurisprudence to support their request and state that in circumstances where the facts and the authors are identical, victims who were not part of the initial complaint can be made to become part of the case if the matter has not yet been considered at the merits stage.

The Complainants allege that the Respondent State reneged on its obligations under the provisions of this Article of the Charter as it failed to take the necessary measures to protect the inhabitants of Kilwa from the violations committed by the Anvil Mining Company which was complicit in the violations with the Armed Forces of the DRC (FARDC). They also aver that by failing to conduct investigations into the events which occurred in Kilwa, the State also gave up on its obligations under the same provisions. Finally, the Complainants contend that it was incumbent on the Respondent State under the conditions set out in Article 1 of the Charter to award the victims fair and adequate reparation.

In order to establish the relationship between the Respondent State, particularly through the FARDC, and the Anvil Mining Company, the Complainants mention the report of the United Nations Mission in Congo (MONUC) which attests to the fact that the Company in question released its aircrafts to transport at least 150 FARDC soldiers from Lubumbashi to Kilwa, its vehicles for the conduct of operations in the town and to transport arrested civilians to detention centres for them to be tortured or sent to mass graves for execution and also to transport corpses from homes, streets or places of detention to mass graves. The same vehicles and earth-moving machines were used to bury the victims, loot and take away people's property.
The Complainants conclude that the authorities of the Respondent State were not only informed but were also directly involved in the violation of the obligation under Article 1 of the Charter.

Regarding the violation of this right, the Complainants cite cases of summary executions and killings, enforced disappearances, drowning and the disproportionate use of force. They provide the testimony of X, a victim who survived the summary executions and therefore an eye-witness to the executions. X witnessed the transportation of dozens of civilians to graves on the outskirts of Kilwa where they were executed while kneeling down. The bullet aimed at X did not hit him and he escaped after the departure of the FARDC but MMM, the son of his neighbour LLL, was executed. Victim Y survived under similar circumstances.

The Complainants further mention the circumstances of the execution of MMM, the 12-year old son of LLL. MMM was arrested while returning from school and executed. LLL could not recover the corpse for fear that he would be arrested. The funeral could not be organised because the said Adémar, a FARDC officer, prevented them from doing so.

Regarding the victim MPWETO Malangisha Pélagie, in her attempt to escape, she left behind her brother NYEMBO Lenge, a mentally-challenged person. He was killed by FARDC soldiers and thrown into a mass grave. NNN witnessed her daughter being raped and sexually abused by Col Adémar's men. Similarly, the Complainants produce testimonies of the parents of two young men, OOO, a 19-year old, and PPP, a 21-year old, who were executed by the FARDC.

The Complainants cite the testimony of FARAY MWAYUMA Adèle who lost her two sons, ULIMWENGU LUKUMANI and ULIMWENGU NOMBELE, who stayed back in Kilwa to protect the family's property. They are missing, and survivor X testified that all civilians who remained in the town when the FARDC arrived were arrested and executed by Colonel Adémar's troops.

Concerning the cases of death by drowning, the Complainants contend that they are attributable to the FARDC since the civilians concerned attempted to escape in dozens by lake from Kilwa to Zambia. Witness AAA reports that the FARDC fired shells that caused the boats to capsize and prompted the deaths by drowning. AAA lost her baby of a few months old under these circumstances. The body of the baby, BBB, was recovered and buried by villagers in a village called Kalaso. CCC, the father of AAA, corroborates her testimony and explains that 12 of his close family members were in a boat in which BBB, EEE, FFF, GGG, HHH, III, JJJ and KKK died by drowning.

The allegation of violation of the right protected under this Article focuses mainly on the case of KUNDA MUSOPELO Pierre, the chief of police in Kilwa. The Complainants allege that the victim was arrested as a result of a personal conflict he had with Colonel Adémar; that he was transferred to Lubumbashi, held in incommunicado detention for three months and only authorised his family to meet him upon the insistence of MONUC. Members of his family testified that he had lost weight, walked and talked with pain and complained of harsh treatment meted out to him during his detention.

The victim was not reinstated in the police force after his release in spite of the fact that the Military Court had declared him innocent. He also did not receive any further benefits even though he had served in the Congolese police force for more than 15 years. At the time of his arrest, he was owed three months' salary arrears which were never paid to him even four years after the events. He was married, a father of three children and his family is living in a very deplorable situation and is unable to cater for themselves since they all depended entirely on him.

The Complainants further allege that the population of Kilwa was generally subjected to inhuman and degrading treatment through bombardments, forced exile, disappearances, looting and fear of reprisals or new violations. They also mention the impossibility for survivors to mourn their dead ones in a dignified manner.

On the allegation of violation of this provision of the Charter, the Complainants submit that KUNDA MUSOPELO Pierre was arrested for no reason and held in incommunicado detention for close to three months without being brought before a judge for trial.

The Complainants contend that the proceedings at the Military Courts were marked by a series of violations. They cite, among others, the questioning of victims without their lawyers whereas accused persons were assisted and the impossibility for several witnesses to enjoy the services of interpreters. They were interrogated in French whereas the majority of them speak Bemba.

Moreover, the Complainants indicate that key witnesses were not heard during the public hearings in Kilwa, especially a driver at the Anvil Mining Company and Red Cross workers who did not attend the hearings for fear of reprisals. MONUC criticised the court for harassing the victims during the same hearings. One of them was threatened with death after protesting against the refusal of the judge to admit his testimony.

The Complainants further contend that before, during and after the trial, human rights defenders, the victims, their witnesses and human rights organisations that supported them were harassed and threatened. They cite, among others, the case of the organisation ASADHO/Katanga.

According to the Complainants, the most alarming of all is that in spite of the numerous and tangible evidence, the Military Court concluded that all persons who died during the events were fighting for the Revolutionary Movement for the Liberation of Katanga (MRLK), that people's property was destroyed by the MRLK and that no summary execution was carried out in Kilwa. They claim that all the FARDC members have been absolved.

The Complainants submit that Ms Louise Arbour, the then United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights, in a statement, expressed surprise at the verdict of the military courts in spite of the serious violations deliberately committed. The Complainants are of the view that the decision of the Military High Court to dismiss the appeal of the victims is also a violation of the right to a fair trial. They submit that the grounds for the said dismissal of the appeal, among others, are the lack of special powers of attorney from the victims' lawyers whereas the same lawyers had represented the victims in the courts of first instance; the fact that the Military Prosecutor was said to have a lower rank than the main defendant; meanwhile the said prosecutor had acted in that capacity throughout the proceedings without any objection from the court. The Complainants contend that these grounds are a violation of the right to appeal.

The Complainants refer to the immense pressure put on the military prosecutor, Colonel NZABI MBOMBO, to compel him to drop the charges levelled against the workers of Anvil Mining, as a violation of Article 26 of the Charter. They allege that his refusal to give in to the pressure led to his transfer to another court. The Complainants further cite the letter of the United Nations Special Rapporteur on the Independence of Judges, which stated that "the acquittal of all the accused persons in spite of the huge evidence produced, including eyewitness accounts and the changes made at the helm of the judiciary in the DRC seem to portray that the independence of judges was not respected in the trial". The Complainants submit that the Special Rapporteur laid emphasis on the transfer of the military prosecutor mid-way into the trial.

The Complainants cite several testimonies confirming that the widespread bombings in Kilwa and the looting carried out by members of the FARDC caused the destruction or the confiscation of more than 200 houses and lots of property according to MONUC. Cash was extorted from traders. People lost not only their personal effects but property used in income-generating activities. They cite the case of FARAY MWAYUMA Adèle's family which, among others, lost fishing nets, a diesel engine, two car batteries, goats, chicken, agricultural products, bags of salt and other items and products used in commercial activities carried out by the family. Following this loss, the family experienced very difficult living conditions.
The Complainants further contend that the destruction of houses is also a violation of the right to housing.

To buttress the allegation of violation, the Complainants claim that the destruction and looting of property deprived the people of their means of carrying out activities which helped them to survive. They allege that the right to economic development has been violated, given that the bombings and looting of working tools used for the production of services and agriculture have undermined economic activities. The Complainants contend that this situation has brought about unemployment and poverty among the people.

Regarding denial of the right to cultural development and respect for identity, they refer to the violation of the right to funeral rites, which is very important in African societies. The Complainants contend that burial in mass graves is an affront to African values and traditions, given that in the societies concerned, it is only after sepulchres have been constructed that the parents of the deceased can mourn and conduct traditional burial rites for the repose of the souls of the departed. The Complainants assert that this is the tradition in the DRC in general, and especially among the Babemba community in Kilwa.

As indicated under the procedure, the Secretariat complied with all the requirements in the Commission's Rules of Procedure in transmitting the Complainants' merits submissions to the Respondent State. In spite of its compliance with the relevant procedure, the Respondent State did not transmit any observations.

The Commission has established the practice of issuing a default judgment whenever a Respondent State fails to submit. On the basis of its jurisprudence and the findings noted under the procedure, the Commission decides to consider the merits of this Communication.

On this issue, the Commission notes that it has accepted the joinder of parties, particularly in the case of Haregewoin Gebresellaise and Institute for Human Rights & Development in Africa v. Ethiopia and this is generally done on the basis of its human rights protection mandate. That said, in considering in particular the substantive conditions for admitting third parties, the Commission took into account the similarity of the facts, prayers and identical nature of the issues of law or fact in respect of the said requests. It also considered that the most relevant provisions being the joinder of Communications, the same should also apply to the joinder of Parties.

In this case, the beneficiaries and victims whose joinder is requested are natives of Kilwa, and they allege to have experienced the same events as the initial victims. Even if their requests are different, which is based on a certain logic, the facts, their authors and the questions of law raised by these requests contain a certain degree of similarity to the extent that it is appropriate to join them to the main case. The Commission thus decides to grant the requests for a joinder with all the related legal implications.

The Commission notes that in addition to the allegations of violations of the provisions of Articles 1, 4, 5, 6, 7(1), 14 and 26, the Complainants extend their submissions and prayers to include Article 22 of the Charter. According to the Commission's established practice, additional claims can be accepted as long as they are based on the same facts and do not undermine issues already resolved at the admissibility stage, and that they can be substantiated by the author and cannot be successfully disputed by the opposing party.

The Commission has established the similarity and identical nature of the facts above. It further notes that the Complainants have supported the allegations of violation of Article 22 and will consider the related submissions under its analysis on the merits. Given that the Respondent State received ample notification of the procedure and the evidence of the case, the Commission is in a position to deliver a default judgment. As such, the question of opportunity for a response from the opposing party does not arise. Finally, it emerges from the consideration of the request for a joinder of the parties that the conclusions on admissibility are applicable to the new submissions and prayers. The Commission thus concludes that the said claims should be admitted and considered

The Commission clearly established in Social and Economic Rights Action Center (SERAC) and Center for Economic and Social Rights (CESR) v. Nigeria that States Parties to the African Charter have the four duties of respect, protect, promote and fulfill the rights guaranteed in the Charter. With respect to Article 1 the contention of the complainant largely relate to the duties of respect and protect. As the Commission in the SERAC case stated, the duty to respect entails that the State should refrain from interfering in the enjoyment of all fundamental rights; it should respect right-holders, their freedoms, autonomy, resources, and liberty of their action. Applied to the facts in the current communication, the state is to be considered responsible for breaching the duty to respect when any of its agents, in the instant case the FARDC, interfered with or violated the rights of affected people.

Additionally and equally importantly, the complainants alleged that the Anvil Mining Company was involved in the perpetration of the alleged violations of various rights under the African Charter. Although this raises the question of the responsibility of the multinational corporation for violations of rights guaranteed in the African Charter, principally it concerns the duty of the state to protect. This duty entails that the state takes all necessary steps to safeguard against human rights abuses by third parties, including corporations, including through taking measures for preventing, investigating, punishing and providing redress for victims. With respect to the role of the mining company, following its finding in the SERAC et al v. Nigeria, the Commission emphasizes the necessity and legal imperative that entities engaged in the extractive industries undertake their operations with due regard to the rights of the host communities. At the minimum they should avoid from engaging in activities having the effect of bringing about violations of the rights of the members of the communities in the areas of their operation. This includes not participating in or supporting the perpetration of violations of human and peoples' rights.

As the uncontested facts presented by the complainants revealed, in the instant case, not only has the State failed in respect of its duty to respect as noted above, it also failed in respect of its duty to protect. It failed not only to investigate and punish the involvement of the Anvil Mining Company but also to provide redress for the victims against the Company for the role it played in the perpetration of the violations. As a result, the State was in breach of its obligations under Article 1 of the African Charter.

According to the provisions of the said Article, "Human beings are inviolable. Every human being shall be entitled to respect for his life and the integrity of his person. No one may be arbitrarily deprived of this right". Concerning the violations of the right to life as guaranteed by the Charter, the Complainants cited summary executions and killings, enforced disappearances, deaths by drowning and the use of excessive force.

Regarding summary executions and killings, the Commission has consistently maintained in its jurisprudence that it is a flagrant violation of the provisions of Article 4. Among others, in SERAC v. Nigeria, the Commission concluded that Article 4 makes it mandatory for the State party to prohibit arbitrary killings by agents of the State and for the public authorities to strictly control the conditions under which a person may be deprived of his life.

In this case, the Commission notes that the reported facts reveal bombardments of the civilian population, arrests followed by extrajudicial killings, all actions that constitute a violation of Article 4. The arguments made by the military courts seem to establish that these actions were justified as a result of the participation of the entire population of Kilwa in an uprising instigated by the MRLK Movement. Apart from the fact that such an assumption is materially unlikely, nothing justified the widespread bombardment and the execution, outside any legal procedure, of a large number of civilians including women and children.

The Commission notes that whatever the causes of the deaths of persons who fled the town of Kilwa in the circumstances of this case, there is a direct causal relationship between the bombardments and the abuses perpetrated against the targeted population. The deaths that occurred by drowning, followed by the firing of shells at the boats transporting the people fleeing fall under this category. The same situation applies to the enforced disappearances since the victims have still not returned to their families almost five years after the events. The testimonies of the survivors confirm such a conclusion.

Having established the facts as constituting a violation of the right to life, before establishing the violation of this right by the Respondent State, it is important to conclude on the responsibility of the latter. In this regard, the Commission recalls that the principle is the presumption that the Respondent State is responsible as long as one of its institutions or one of its authorities failed in its obligation to respect, protect or enforce the right concerned. The imputability of the actions of individuals assigned to carry out a task finds its source in the fact that the Respondent State is a single entity in international law. In this case, the violations committed by the FARDC are inevitably attributable to the Respondent State.

The subsequent issue is one of prior imputability of such actions to Colonel Adémar and the forces he commanded during the intervention in Kilwa. In this regard, the Commission notes that a broad range of proof and circumstantial evidence have been produced to demonstrate such imputability. In the first place, it observes that many inhabitants of Kilwa, among other survivors and families of the executed victims, provided testimonies about seeing FARDC members. Heads of international organisations and non-governmental organisations such as MONUC and ASADHO confirmed this fact. Finally, credible authorities from the United Nations, in particular the High Commissioner for Human Rights and the Special Rapporteur on the Independence of Judges also confirmed the imputability of the abuses to FARDC members.

Even though the local courts themselves have confirmed the intervention by the FARDC, they however found the absolute lack of responsibility on the part of the FARDC members who were prosecuted. The Commission already concluded above that, looking at the flagrant and the internationally-publicised nature of the facts, it was probably erroneous to conclude that all the civilians were parties to the conflict and that there was no single case of summary execution. Even if that was the case, the summary execution of civilians arrested but who were not participating in or no longer in the combat would all the same amount to arbitrariness, which is prohibited by the Charter interpreted together with the relevant provisions of international humanitarian law. Moreover, the violations of Article 4 mentioned above are attributable to the Respondent State through the direct responsibility of members of the armed forces, in this case the FARDC. The Commission thus concludes that the Respondent State has violated the provisions of Article 4 of the Charter.
The provisions of Article 5 guarantee the respect for human dignity and prohibit torture and inhuman or degrading treatment.

In its jurisprudence, the European Court of Human Rights considered "torture" to mean "any act by which severe pain or suffering, whether physical or mental, is intentionally inflicted on a person for a specific purpose". The United Nations Committee against Torture notes in its General Comment No. 20 that the offences committed must cause atrocious suffering inflicted intentionally, with the aim of extracting information or confessions, punish the victim for real or alleged acts and be imputable to a State official or a person acting in that capacity. The Commission adopts this position in its decision in Sudan Human Rights Organisation and Another v. Sudan.

Concerning acts that can fall within the scope of the above list, the Commission concluded in the cases of Malawi African Association and Others v. Mauritania and Achuthan and Amnesty International v. Malawi that the fact of being buried and burned or better still the deliberate refusal by police officers to give victims access to health facilities constituted acts of torture. The Commission will first of all consider the case of KUNDA MUSOPELO Pierre before considering the case of the population of Kilwa.

Concerning KUNDA MUSOPELO Pierre, who at the time of the events was the Kilwa Police Chief, it has to be determined whether his incommunicado detention for three months, without contact with his family and the cruel treatment meted out to him during the said detention constituted inhuman and degrading treatment. The Commission notes that the said treatment includes the fact of having been beaten and whipped. The treatment was inflicted by FARDC members who accused the officer of having supported the Revolutionary Movement for the Liberation of Katanga (MRLK). In the light of the above-mentioned facts and circumstances of the case, the Commission concludes that there were acts of torture.

In Modise v. Botswana and Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights and Interights v. Egypt, the Commission considers that inhuman and degrading treatment essentially violates human dignity. Logically, torture violates dignity all the more. Consequently, there is the need to conclude on the violation of the right to dignity of the individual in the case of KUNDA MUSOPELO Pierre.

Regarding the argument that there was inhuman and degrading treatment against the population of Kilwa, the Commission recalls its position in the case of Sudan Human Rights Organisation and Centre on Housing Rights and Evictions (COHRE) v. Sudan in which it concluded that the fact that the Respondent State, in its attempt to fight the Janjaweed militia, targeted the civilian population, thus causing their forced exodus constituted inhuman treatment under Article 5 of the Charter. The conclusions as to the violation of the right to dignity of KUNDA MUSOPELO Pierre are also applicable to the entire population of Kilwa who had to flee from their homes and lived in exile under precarious conditions. It is therefore appropriate to conclude that Article 5 was violated in their case.

Article 6 of the Charter states that: "Every individual shall have the right to liberty and to the security of his person. No one may be deprived of his freedom except for reasons and conditions previously laid down by law, in particular, no one may be arbitrarily arrested or detained". The Complainants allege that KUNDA MUSOPELO Pierre was arbitrarily detained. The issue is to determine whether the victim's detention was based on and conducted under conditions previously laid down by law.

In the case of Ouko v. Kenya where the Complainant was detained for a period of ten (10) months without trial, the Commission was of the view that the detention was arbitrary. It further concluded in Free Legal Assistance Group and Others v. Zaire that detention for an indefinite period of time was a violation of the provisions of Article 6 of the Charter. In particular, in Liesbeth Zegveld and Mussie Ephrem v. Eritrea, the Commission adopted the position that incommunicado detention is arbitrary.

Furthermore, the Commission considers that, as maintained by the United Nations Human Rights Committee in Gorji-Dinka v. Cameroon, an assessment from the legal perspective as suggested by Article 6 of the Charter must be based on the necessity and reasonableness in all circumstances and not necessarily as being "contrary to the law".

In the circumstances of the case, the Commission notes that the victim's detention lasted for more than three months without the victim appearing before a judge or having any contact with his family. Furthermore, the main reason for his detention was his alleged participation in the activities of the MRLK insurrectionist movement, reasons which the Commission has earlier dismissed as irrelevant. The fact that the interested party was subsequently tried and acquitted does not make any difference in this case in view of the fact that the arbitrary detention was already established before the military courts' proceedings began. The Commission thus finds that Article 6 of the Charter was violated. The findings of the Commission regarding the responsibility of the Respondent State for violating Article 4 also apply concerning the violation of Article 6. The same further apply in the cases of the civilians detained by FARDC members under similar circumstances such as victims X and Y.

Article 7(1) of the African Charter guarantees the right to have one's cause heard in accordance with due process. Regarding the violation of the right to a fair trial, the Complainants alleged in particular the interrogations which were conducted in the absence of lawyers, lack of translation into a language understood by the victims, exclusion and threats against key witnesses and organisations supporting them, and finally the acquittal of all FARDC members in spite of the tangible and convincing evidence corroborated by witnesses, including United Nations agencies. Based on the submissions of the Complainants, the Commission is of the view that it is appropriate to consider the two fundamental rights, which include the right to defence (Article 7(1)(c)) and the right to an appeal (Article 7(1)(a)).

Concerning the right to defence, the Commission is of the view that it was not respected in the situations where the alleged victim was denied assistance by his counsels as it was the case in the cases of Saro-Wiwa v. Nigeria and Avocats Sans Frontières (on behalf of Bwampamiye) v. Burundi. Indeed, the right to defence derives from the need for the person charged or accused to enjoy the services of a specialist (counsel) and be informed of the procedure and substantive issues in order for his rights to be guaranteed.

The same analysis applies to the need to communicate with the accused person in a language he understands throughout the proceedings. Recalling its Principles and Guidelines on the Right to a Fair Trial and Legal Assistance in Africa, the Commission arrived at a similar conclusion in the case of Titanji Duga Ernest (on behalf of Cheonumu Martin and Others) v. Cameroon. In this case, the victims were all English-speaking and were interrogated in French.

Even though the right to witnesses, both prosecution and defence witnesses, particularly the right to summon, examine and cross-examine witnesses is not explicitly stipulated in Article 7 of the Charter, the corresponding standards of this Article in other Conventions confirm that such a right is covered by the provisions of Article 7(1)(c) of the Charter, i.e. the right to defence. The European Court of Human Rights has consistently found a violation of this express right under the provisions of Article 6(3)(d) of the Convention, as it was the case in Lucà v. Italy and Solakov v. the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia.

The Commission notes that in the circumstances of this Communication, many witnesses and victims were interrogated in Swahili in the absence of their lawyers whereas they spoke only Bemba, and that key witnesses were not heard as a result of the judge's refusal and other threats. These elements point to a violation of the right to defence protected under Article 7(1)(c) of the Charter.

Regarding the alleged violation of the right to an appeal, the Commission notes that the Principles and Guidelines on the Right to a Fair Trial in Africa underscores "the entitlement to a decision delivered without undue delay with adequate notice of and reasons for the delay" as an essential element of the right to a fair hearing in general. Furthermore, there is a logical connection between the right to a reasoned decision and the right to an appeal as recalled by the Commission in Good v. Botswana and Amnesty International v. Zambia. Such a position is consistent with the practice of the European Court of Human Rights and the Inter-American Court of Human Rights.

The importance of sufficient and relevant grounds for judicial decisions is confirmed in the practice of national courts. In this regard, it is worthy to mention that in the case of Dibagula v. The Republic, the Court of Appeal of Tanzania found a violation of the right to a fair trial, stating that: "The necessity for courts to give reasons for their decisions is borne out of the fact that the reasons introduce clarity and minimise the chances of arbitrariness". The Court of Appeal consequently concluded that the trial judge framed irrelevant issues and failed to attempt to discuss those issues.
Moreover, failure to state reasons is likely to violate the right to an appeal. The European Court of Human Rights confirms this in its decisions in the cases of K.K. v. France and Baucher v. France.

In the present Communication, two major elements are to be assessed in the light of these principles. They include the decision of the military courts to acquit the FARDC members of all charges and the decision to dismiss the victims' appeal for lack of possession of powers of attorney by the lawyers.

Regarding the decision of the military courts, the Commission has already concluded on the implausibility of their conclusions regarding the establishment of the violations and involvement of the FARDC. The judgment of the trial military court indicated that the court summarily found that none of the accused members of the FARDC is guilty, and that the violations did not take place or cannot be imputed to them and that all persons arrested or executed were killed while taking part in combat operations on behalf of the insurrectionist movement.

The Commission notes that the Military High Court, sitting as an Appeals Court confirmed the first decision in spite of the numerous testimonies of survivors, of beneficiaries of the deceased persons, employees of Anvil Mining Company, officials of the United Nations, representatives of MONUC, the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights and the United Nations Special Rapporteur on the Independence of Judges. These elements lead to a legitimate suspicion of glaring shortcomings regarding the relevance of the reasons given in the decisions of the national courts. Such conclusions obviously portray non-compliance with the obligation for national courts to provide reasons for their decisions.

Moreover, concerning the appeal procedure, the Commission notes that the Military High Court dismissed the Complainants' appeal on the grounds that the victims' lawyers did not have powers of attorney while the same lawyers represented their clients in the proceedings before the trial court. The military prosecutor experienced a similar situation when it was stated that he was of a lower rank compared to the main defendant. The Commission's findings on the lack of reasons for the decisions of the national courts apply to this issue. Moreover, these conclusions were a denial of the right to appeal in the circumstances of this case. As such, the Commission concludes that the provisions of Article 7(1)(a) of the Charter have been violated.

This Article essentially imposes an obligation on the Respondent State to guarantee the independence of the courts. The Commission noted in the case of Meldrum v. Zimbabwe that the independence of the courts necessarily presupposes the lack of pressure or interference. The allegation of a violation of Article 26 of the Charter gives the impression of interference by the Respondent State or its institutions.

In this case, it is the transfer of the military prosecutor that is being questioned. In this regard, the Commission notes that the independence of members of the prosecution is a sensitive issue, particularly in African States with a civil law tradition inherited from the continental or French legal and judicial system. In this system, just like in the case of the Respondent State, it is the prosecutor, a magistrate working in the Prosecutor's Office, who represents the people under the direct authority of the Minister of Justice who is a member of the executive arm of government. This authority of the executive arm can give instructions to the magistrate of the Office of the Prosecutor who is also vested with functions and powers of a judicial nature.

This state of affairs obviously undermines the independence of justice delivery and judicial authorities as has consistently been noted by the European Court of Human Rights. Such was the case in the two decisions of principle delivered notably against France, whose judicial system particularly in the area of prosecution was inherited by African civil law courts. In fact, in the cases of Medvedyev v. France and Moulin v. France, which were decided in 2008 and 2010 respectively, the Court noted that the Attorney General cannot be considered as a judicial authority and cannot exercise such functions for lack of independence from the executive arm.

In this case, information contained in the submissions indicates that Colonel NZABI MBOMBO, Senior Military Prosecutor, who was in charge of the case and brought the matter before the trial courts was recalled to Kinshasa and reassigned to Kananga while the trial was on-going. In the circumstances where the said judicial officer had conducted all the investigations in Kilwa and was in possession of all the details of the case, his transfer while the trial was in progress shows the absolute control of the executive power over the course of justice, including the lack of concern for the interest of litigants while exercising such control. The Commission notes that under these circumstances, there was necessarily a conflict of interest to the detriment of the victims as demonstrated by the impossibility of independence of the prosecuting and investigating authority. It is thus appropriate to conclude that Article 26 of the Charter was violated.

Article 14 of the Charter stipulates that: "The right to property shall be guaranteed. It may only be encroached upon in the interest of public need or in the general interest of the community and in accordance with the provisions of the appropriate laws". The Commission has earlier indicated that the acts constituted abuses against civilian victims. Consequently, expropriation in the interest of public need must be discounted.

In the present Communication, regarding a subsequent violation to those established by the Commission above, it is sufficient to point out the nature of the property looted and their imputability to the Respondent State. The issue of imputability has been addressed above. Regarding the nature of the property looted, the Commission notes that, as stated by the Complainants and confirmed by some international organizations, particularly the United Nations, the FARDC members caused a lot of material damage following the bombardments carried out in the residential and commercial areas.

They subsequently looted, in a systematic fashion, more than 200 homes according to MONUC sources, including extortion of goods and income from commercial activities. Means of production were also destroyed, thus undermining income-generating activities. These destructions obviously constitute a violation of the right to property as guaranteed by the Charter for individuals, in particular, and for the Kilwa population as a whole, regarding public property and infrastructure. Given that the buildings destroyed served mainly as homes and that the population concerned was forced to flee the town, it is appropriate to further conclude that the right to housing was violated.

Under the relevant provisions of Article 22, all peoples shall have the right to their economic, social and cultural development with due regard to their freedom and identity and in the equal enjoyment of the common heritage of mankind. The Complainants allege a violation of the right to economic and cultural development.

For the purpose of a judicious consideration of the arguments to back this allegation, there is need to clarify the meaning of the right to development under the provisions of Article 22 of the Charter. The provision stipulates that: "All peoples shall have the right to their development...." Reference to peoples may be understood to mean that it is necessary to have the status of people, in the sense of ethnic or national group, or indigenous community, in order to enjoy this right.

The Commission in the communication Sudan Human Rights Organization and Centre on Housing Rights and Evictions (COHRE) v. Sudan held that 'to determine violation of this article (Article 22), the Commission will first have to determine whether the victims constitute a 'people' within the context of the African Charter.' The Commission went on to say that 'An important aspect of this process of defining "a people" is the characteristics, which a particular people may use to identify themselves, through the principle of self identification, or be used by other people to identify them. These characteristics, include the language, religion, culture, the territory they occupy in a state, common history, ethno - anthropological factors, to mention but a few. In States with mixed racial composition, race becomes a determinant of groups of "peoples", just as ethnic identity can also be a factor.'

In the instant case, while providing materials for establishing that the victims form part of a people within the framework of Article remains important, the lack of such materials does not by itself alone preclude the application of Article 22. The fact that the right to development is conceived as a right of peoples under Article 22 does not preclude the exercise of this right by individuals. The Commission thus agrees with the doctrine that the meaning of the right to development must "closely combine the individual and collective dimensions, since trying to consider only the collective aspect will compromise individual freedoms".

After understanding this subjective perspective of the right to development, there is need to understand it in its substantial nature, in this case its economic and cultural nature which the Complainants allege to have been violated. In its jurisprudence, the Commission has expressed an opinion on the economic and cultural aspects of the right to development under Article 22 of the Charter. Regarding cultural development, it is worthy to recall the decision in Democratic Republic of Congo v. Burundi, Rwanda and Uganda in which the Commission notes that the fact that the Respondent States buried in mass graves the victims of massacres perpetrated by them is a "violation of the right of the Congolese people to cultural development" against the population of the Eastern province of the Complainant.

Such a meaning of the right to cultural development is in conformity with the approach adopted by UNESCO which, in the 2007 Fribourg Declaration on Cultural Rights, states that: "The term "culture" covers those values, beliefs ... traditions ... through which a person or a group expresses ... the meanings that they give to their existence and to their development." The Declaration further states that: ""Cultural community" connotes a group of persons who share ... a common cultural identity that they intend to preserve and develop".

As concerns economic development, in Gunne and Others v. Cameroon, even though the Commission could not find a violation of Article 22 for lack of evidence, it however noted that the acts of "economic marginalisation and the lack of economic infrastructure", if established, would have constituted a violation of the right to development. On the other hand, in the case of Open Society Justice Initiative v. Côte d'Ivoire, the Commission found a violation of the right to economic development on the grounds that the denial to grant people of the Dioula ethnic group nationality and identification documents prevented them from participating in and enjoying the economic development of Côte d'Ivoire. The Commission further noted "the need to ensure a gradual implementation - by creating a conducive environment - and to immediately recommend that individual and collective right to development should be respected, protected and promoted."

In the present Communication, the Commission is of the view that logically, the destruction of property of economic nature or for economic use inevitably has negative economic consequences. This applies to the property destroyed in this case, which contributed directly to income-generating activities, and thus in realising the right of the people of Kilwa to participate in and enjoy economic development. The property destroyed includes personal assets and other infrastructure such as schools and health centres used by the entire Kilwa community. In these circumstances and in the light of the meaning developed above, the right to economic development of the people of Kilwa has been violated.

From a cultural perspective, the victims were buried in mass graves and were consequently deprived of sepulchres worthy of their humanity in accordance with their cultural and ritual practices. Family members were denied the right to perform for their deceased relatives the requisite rites in accordance with the practices recognised in the Democratic Republic of Congo and in particular among the Babemba community in Kilwa. In the circumstances of the case and in the light of the meaning of the right to cultural development developed above, the Commission finds that the cultural aspect of the right under Article 22 of the Charter has been violated.

In accordance with the Commission's established jurisprudence, the violation of rights guaranteed by the Charter entails the right to reparation, including financial compensation, though the Complainant can be requested to assess the damages and provide evidence.

The Commission notes that the Complainants produce a detailed inventory with costs of the damages caused, including evidence provided by some survivors and beneficiaries. The related requests have been stated under the summary of the Complaint. The amounts requested range between 180,000 to 200,000 dollars for the survivors and 300,000 dollars for the deceased persons. The beneficiaries of Commissioner KUNDA MUSOPELO are requesting for 325,000 dollars for arbitrary detention, looting of their property and salary arrears due the victim before his demise.

The Commission notes that even though the purpose of compensation in human rights disputes is not necessarily punitive, money can heal wounds. Regarding the amounts claimed, the Commission notes that they were substantiated and is of the view that no financial compensation can make up for human lives lost. As such, it concludes that is appropriate to grant compensation.

The Complainants requested for public apologies. This type of reparation can serve several purposes, including psychological healing of the victims, promoting social justice, restoring societal balance and changing behaviours. Its implementation indicates the need to take into account the importance of apologies in the understanding of the victim and the perception they have about it. In general, the public image of the victim was undermined and this explains the frequent recourse to this mode of reparation in cases of defamation. The choice of mechanisms and stakeholders to implement this form of reparation is also crucial to its effectiveness.

In this case, the dignity of the population of Kilwa was violated. Given the serious and massive nature of the violations, the Commission is of the view that the implementation of the subsequent decision should include the reconstruction of a rehabilitation project in Kilwa. In reality, this will entail establishing a successful psychological and social healing and rehabilitation process, for which public acknowledgement of the violations is likely to play a crucial role.

Regarding the general requests made by the Complainants, the Commission notes that dozens of other persons are directly concerned by the facts considered in this Communication. This is a public interest litigation case which should benefit all other victims who were not party to the Communication. All the collective requests made are relevant in this regard. For the above reasons, the Commission:

Finds that the Democratic Republic of Congo has violated the provisions of Articles 1, 4, 5, 6, 7(1)(a), 7(1)(c), 14, 22 and 26 of the Charter and the right to housing. As a result, the African Commission: i. Requests the Democratic Republic of Congo to take the necessary steps to prosecute and punish State employees and personnel of the Anvil Mining Company involved in the said violations. ii. Requests the Democratic Republic of Congo to award compensation amounting to USD 200,000 each to Victim X and Victim Y. iii. Urges the Democratic Republic of Congo to award compensation amounting to USD 300,000 to each victim, namely FARAY MWAYUMA Adèle for the loss of each of her sons in addition to USD 30,000 for her looted property; MPWETO Malangisha Pélagie for the loss of her brother, NYEMBO Lenge; LLL for the loss of his son; CCC for the loss of 7 members of his family in addition to USD 5,000 for his looted property; and AAA for the loss of her few months old baby who died by drowning. iv. Requests the Democratic Republic of Congo to award compensation amounting to USD 325,000 to KUNDA Kikumbi Dickay, son of KUNDA MUSOPELO Pierre, representing the KUNDA family. v. Requests the Democratic Republic of Congo, as part of collective reparation, to:- Officially present and publish a full apology to the population of Kilwa. - Conduct an independent inquiry in order to clarify the fate of missing persons and award compensation to their beneficiaries. - Conduct a head count of all the victims who are not party to this Communication towards awarding them fair and adequate compensation for the damages suffered. - Take steps to exhume the bodies buried in mass graves at NSENSELE and give them a dignified burial. - Erect a memorial at NSENSELE in honour of the deceased and missing victims. - Rehabilitate the socio-economic infrastructure destroyed during the events, particularly the Kilwa school and hospital, road and waterway access, the poor state of which facilitated the violations. - Provide adequate psycho-social support to the victims and other inhabitants of Kilwa to enable them overcome the trauma caused by the events. vi. Requests the Democratic Republic of Congo to ensure that the implementation of this decision is monitored by a Monitoring Committee comprising the representatives of the victims and their beneficiaries and the Member of the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights responsible for human rights in the DRC. vii. Requests the Democratic Republic of Congo to report in writing, within one hundred and eighty (180) days, on the measures taken to implement these recommendations. Adopted at the 20 Extraordinary Session of the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights held in Banjul, Republic of The Gambia, from 9 to 18 June 2016

Le 9 novembre 2010, le Secrétariat de la Commission africaine des droits de l'homme et des peuples (le Secrétariat) a reçu de Maître Théogène Muhayeyezu, de nationalité rwandaise, une Plainte introduite sur le fondement des articles 55 de la Charte africaine des droits de l'homme et des peuples (la Charte africaine). Le Plaignant est avocat au Barreau du Rwanda.
La Communication a été introduite contre la République du Rwanda (Etat Partie à la Charte africaine et ci-après dénommée le Rwanda).

Le Plaignant expose qu'au cours de l'année 1994, la Société BP-FINA lui a accordé un crédit d'une valeur totale de 7 867 939 francs rwandais représentant des produits pétroliers d'une valeur de 6 922 253 francs et des frais de transport estimés à 945 686 francs. Aux dires du Plaignant, ce crédit devait être remboursé après la vente du carburant, par le biais de virements bancaires sur un compte ouvert par la Société BP-FINA à la Banque Commerciale du Rwanda (BCR).

En exécution de cet engagement, le Plaignant rapporte avoir versé sur ledit compte un montant de 5 402 615 francs mais que profitant de son absence du Rwanda au cours de l'année 1996, la Société BP-FINA et la BCR ont augmenté le montant de sa dette en débitant indument le compte en banque indiqué plus haut. Le Plaignant expose ainsi que le 26 septembre 1996 la Société BP-FINA a signé un contrat avec ses associés aux termes duquel la Société SOPEGI dont il est membre devait rembourser à BP-FINA un montant de 4 850 779 francs.

En outre, le 1 janvier 1997, la Société BP-FINA se serait fait remettre par la BCR un montant de 2 000 000 francs sur présentation d'un chèque périmé et non provisionné que le Plaignant avait remis à son créancier en 1994 à titre de garantie de remboursement du crédit octroyé.

En tout, poursuit le Plaignant, la Société BP-FINA se serait fait payer une somme de 12 702 777 francs alors que la créance n'était que de 7 867 939 francs. Le Plaignant dénonce donc ce trop perçu d'un montant de 4 834 838 francs et rapporte qu'en acceptant de payer le chèque sans provision déposé en garanti, la BCR a usé de ce prétexte pour débiter son compte et le placer sur la liste des clients insolvables.

Par suite de ces événements, le Plaignant expose qu'ayant entrepris de se faire réhabiliter dans ses droits, il a recouru aux instances judiciaires du Rwanda sans succès. Il rapporte en l'occurrence que sur les cinq demandes soumises aux juges aucune n'a prospéré, les décisions subséquentes ayant été emailisées de contradictions et d'autres caractérisées par un défaut de motivation. A titre d'illustration, le Plaignant cite l'arrêt R.Com AA 0007/09/CS rendu par la Cour suprême du Rwanda le 9 juillet 2010 par lequel la Cour, tout en considérant les faits tels qu'exposés, s'est pourtant refusée à répondre aux questions soulevées. Selon le Plaignant, la position de la Cour serait en violation de l'article 141 de la Constitution et de l'article 147 du Code de procédure civile, commerciale, sociale et administrative du Rwanda.

Le Plaignant avance que la Cour suprême du Rwanda a réservé le même traitement aux déclarations du témoin Emmanuel Mureramanzi cité dans l'arrêt de la Cour cité supra. Selon lesdites déclarations, en consentant à payer le montant de 4 850 779 francs, les associés du Plaignant n'avaient pas connaissance du chèque de 2 000 000 francs déposé en garantie. Le Plaignant estime à cet égard, qu'il aurait dû revenir à la Cour suprême que la Société BP-FINA s'est fait rembourser un montant de loin supérieur à la créance qu'elle détenait sur lui et qu'il avait droit à la répétition de l'indu aux termes des dispositions des articles 133 et 252 du Livre III du Code civil du Rwanda (CCL III).

Au sujet de la même décision de justice, le Plaignant expose de surcroît que la haute juridiction rwandaise s'est refusée à lui donner raison sur la question de son inscription sur la liste des débiteurs de la Banque Commerciale du Rwanda, décision suite à laquelle il a été condamné par les juridictions inférieures à une amende de 3 000 000 francs. Un tel refus est à tout le moins surprenant selon le Plaignant puisque la Cour suprême elle-même avait dit justement non fondée, car non justifiée, la demande reconventionnelle de la Banque Commerciale du Rwanda tendant à faire reconnaître sa créance sur la personne du Plaignant et les accroissements y afférents.

Le Plaignant avance qu'en conséquence de ce qui précède, la Cour suprême étant la plus haute juridiction de l'Etat défendeur, il est évident que ses biens seront mis en vente pour recouvrer les condamnations des juridictions du fond confirmées par la Cour suprême.

Le Plaignant allègue que les faits énoncés ci-dessus constituent une violation des dispositions des articles 7 et 14 de la Charte africaine. Il demande par conséquent à la Commission de requérir de l'Etat défendeur de : (i) Déclarer que l'affaire a été mal jugée ; (ii) Condamner l'usage par les juridictions de l'Etat défendeur de termes injurieux ; (iii) Accorder une indemnisation matérielle d'un montant de deux cent millions (200 000 000) de francs Rwandais ; (iv) Accorder une indemnisation morale ; et (v) Respecter ses engagements internationaux en garantissant ses droits dans la SOGEPI.

La Plainte est parvenue au Secrétariat le 9 novembre 2010. Lors de sa 48 Session ordinaire tenue du 10 au 24 novembre 2010 à Banjul, en Gambie, la Commission africaine des droits de l'homme et des peuples (la Commission) a examiné la Plainte et décidé de s'en saisir. Le 30 novembre 2010, le Secrétariat a par conséquent informé l'Etat défendeur de la Plainte, lui demandant de soumettre ses observations écrites sur la recevabilité dans un délai de trois mois.

Par Lettre en date du 9 décembre 2010, le Secrétariat a informé le Plaignant de ce que la Commission a décidé de se saisir de la Plainte et qu'elle entend statuer sur la recevabilité lors de sa 49 Session ordinaire prévue pour se tenir du 28 avril au 12 mai 2011 dans un lieu à préciser. Le Plaignant a été invité par la même occasion à transmettre ses arguments sur la recevabilité dans un délai d'un mois.

Lors de sa 49 Session ordinaire, en l'absence de soumission des parties, la Commission a décidé de renvoyer l'examen de la Communication à sa 50 Session ordinaire. Le 2 juin 2011, le Secrétariat a informé les parties de cette décision et leur a accordé un nouveau délai de deux mois pour déposer leurs mémoires sur la recevabilité.

Le 24 juin 2011, en réponse aux correspondances du Secrétariat, le Plaignant a rappelé qu'il avait soumis ses arguments sur la recevabilité à l'occasion de la saisine de la Commission et que lesdits arguments devaient être considérés dans l'examen de la Communication.

Lors de sa 50 Session ordinaire tenue du 24 octobre au 5 novembre 2011 à Banjul, en Gambie, la Commission a décidé d'un renvoi à nouveau. Les parties ont été informées de cette décision et le Secrétariat leur a rappelé de soumettre leurs moyens sur la recevabilité.
