On 23 August 2012, the Secretariat of the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights (the Secretariat) received from Counsel Moualal Ruben, Lawyer at the Cameroon Bar, a Complaint submitted on the basis of Article 55 of the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights (the African Charter).

The Complaint was submitted on behalf of Messrs Samuel Mack-Kit and Priso Moukoko, who were, until August 2011, respectively President and Secretary General of the political party called Union of the Peoples of Cameroon (UPC), against the Republic of Cameroon (a State Party to the African Charter and hereinafter referred to as the Respondent State or Cameroon).

The Complainants state that, created on 10 January 1948 in Douala, the UPC functioned as a political party and carried out activities that led to Cameroon's independence on 1 January 1960 and to the reunification of its two separated parts on 1 October 1960. Banned on 13 July 1955, the party had been rehabilitated by presidential decree of 25 February 1960. Its functioning was however hindered by the harassment of its main leaders until the 1990s.

The Complainants report that, thanks to Law No. 90-56 of 19 December 1990 authorising multipartism in Cameroon, the political parties already existing had obtained legal recognition without needing to fulfil the authorisation formalities again. The only two parties existing at that time, that is the UPC and the Cameroon People's Democratic Movement (CPDM), thus benefited from automatic legal existence under the new legislation.

By virtue of this legal recognition, the Complainants continue, they officially notified the authorities of their intention to carry out their activities and were indeed elected to the national leadership of the UPC. But immediately after the start of their activities, they were subjected to numerous harassments by the Respondent State. They thus report that another group of persons led by Messrs Dicka Akwa and Augustin Frederic Kodock, all from the ruling CPDM, suddenly claimed to belong to the UPC, obtained recognition from the administration and hastened to have the acronym registered as a trademark with the African Intellectual Property Organisation (OAPI).

The leaders of this new "wing or faction" recognised by the administration as the sole leadership of the UPC then prohibited any political use of the acronym and emblems of the party. The Complainants report that, on the basis of such recognition, the State authorities subjected them to a series of police, administrative and judicial harassments.

The Complainants state that, faced with administrative prohibitions on holding any meeting of their party and the police persecution that followed, they created another political party called UPC-Manidem. According to the Complainants, three months after the filing of the authorisation application, the Governor of the Littoral Province had still not responded whereas, under Article 7(2) of the above-cited Law, such silence entailed a deemed legal existence of the party. In response to their correspondence taking note of the legal existence of UPC-Manidem, the State opposed the said recognition on the ground that it was likely to create confusion with the UPC already recognised and whose acronym is protected by OAPI.

The Complainants report that, by Order No. 02/0/PCA/92-93 of 16 December 1992, the Supreme Court annulled the administration's decision rejecting the tacit legal recognition of UPC-Manidem. The third-party opposition brought by the recognised wing of the UPC was declared unfounded by the same court.

Having lost in these proceedings, the wing of the UPC recognised by the administration brought a civil action against the Complainants for use of an acronym protected by OAPI. Having been unsuccessful before the Court of First Instance and the Court of Appeal, the Complainants lodged an appeal on points of law before the Supreme Court in March 1998, with no action taken on it as of the date of seizure of the Commission. In the meantime, the Complainants report, the candidacy of Mr Samuel Mack-Kit for the 2004 presidential election was rejected for lack of investiture by the UPC hierarchy. Likewise, the Supreme Court rejected his application contesting this, for the same reasons as those that had motivated the rejection of his candidacy.

Finally, the Complainants state that in a third set of proceedings, the leaders of the UPC recognised by the administration brought against them a direct summons for unauthorised use of the attributes of the UPC. The Court of First Instance then took seven (07) years, from 2004 to 2011, to respond to their preliminary objections (exceptions in limine litis), the case having been subject to more than 80 adjournments. Having appealed against the decision finally rendered on 24 June 2011, the Complainants had still not obtained a response as of the seizure of the Commission, on 23 August 2012, after a new series of adjournments.
The Complainants allege the violation of the provisions of Articles 2, 3, 7, 9, 10, 11 and 13 of the African Charter.

The Complainants request the Commission to enjoin Cameroon to: - Cease the disturbances and other violations against them in their capacity as leaders of the UPC; - Cease all interference in the affairs of political parties, particularly of the UPC, by seeking to impose a group of men in place of the legitimate leaders of the said party and to its detriment.

The Complaint reached the Secretariat on 23 August 2012. At its 52nd Ordinary Session held from 9 to 22 October 2012, in Yamoussoukro, Côte d'Ivoire, the Commission was seized of the Complaint. On 30 October 2012, the Secretariat informed the Parties of this decision and requested the Complainants' observations on Admissibility.

On 7 January 2013, the Secretariat received the Complainants' observations. The said observations were transmitted to the Respondent State on 4 February 2013. On 5 April 2013, the Respondent State transmitted its brief in defence on the Admissibility of the Communication. On 6 May 2013, the Secretariat transmitted the Respondent State's brief to the Complainants and requested their observations.

At its 54th Ordinary Session held from 22 October to 5 November 2013 in Banjul, The Gambia, the Commission examined the Communication and decided to defer its decision having received the Complainants' observations on the Respondent State's brief. On 23 December 2013, the Parties were duly informed of this decision and the Secretariat again requested the reply of the Complainants.

At its 14th Extraordinary Session (7 to 14 March 2014, Banjul, The Gambia) and 54th Ordinary Session (28 April to 12 May 2014, Luanda, Angola), the Commission deferred its decision on Admissibility owing to time constraints. The Parties were duly informed.

At its 16th Extraordinary Session held from 20 to 29 July 2014 in Kigali, Rwanda, the Commission examined the Communication and declared it admissible. On 4 August 2014, the Secretariat informed the Parties and requested the Complainants' observations on the merits.

The 56th Ordinary Session of the Commission scheduled to be held in October 2014 having been postponed and then cancelled, the Communication could not be examined. At its 17th Extraordinary Session held from 19 to 28 February 2015 in Banjul, The Gambia, the Commission examined the Communication and decided to grant a final period of one month to the Complainants before proceeding to strike the case off the roll.

On 19 March 2015, the Complainants transmitted their observations on the merits. On 13 April 2015, the Secretariat transmitted the Complainants' observations to the Respondent State. On 16 June 2015, the Applicant State requested an additional period of two months to submit its observations on the merits. The Secretariat granted it a period of one month in accordance with the Commission's Rules of Procedure.

On 23 July 2015, the Respondent State transmitted its observations on the merits. The Secretariat transmitted them to the Complainants on 31 July 2015. On expiry of the thirty-day period provided for this purpose by the Rules of Procedure, the Complainants did not transmit a reply.

Of the admissibility requirements provided for in Article 56 of the African Charter, the Complainants dwell in particular on that relating to the exhaustion of local remedies. The arguments they develop in this regard concern, firstly, the administrative procedure relating to the authorisation for the functioning of UPC-Manidem; secondly, the civil and commercial procedure linked to the use of the acronym "UPC"; and thirdly, the direct summons procedure concerning the use of the acronym and emblems of the "UPC".

On the first point, the Complainants recall Order No. 08/0/PCA/SC/93-94 of 13 December 1993 by which the Administrative Chamber of the Supreme Court of Cameroon declared unfounded the third-party opposition brought against its previous Order confirming the tacit authorisation for the functioning of UPC-Manidem. The Complainants allege that the decision of the highest court amounted to the exhaustion of the competent local remedies.

On the second point, the Complainants argue that local remedies existed but were ineffective. In support of this argument, they report that the appeal on points of law lodged before the Supreme Court against Judgment No. 113/C of 20 March 1998 of the Court of Appeal had remained without action as of the date of seizure of the Commission, that is 23 August 2012.

On the third point, the Complainants allege that remedies were available but were abnormally prolonged. They argue in this regard that the case brought against them in court was subject to more than eighty (80) adjournments and remained pending for seven (07) entire years, from September 2004 to June 2011, whereas they had raised only preliminary objections (exceptions in limine litis). In the Complainants' understanding, such a delay abnormally prolonged the local remedies. They go on to allege that once the decision was made on 24 June 2011, the appeal they lodged had not been followed up until the date of seizure of the Commission.

Without contesting the facts as reported by the Complainants, the Respondent State alleges that the Communication does not comply with the requirements laid down in Article 56 of the African Charter. The Respondent State argues that, in addition to the failure to exhaust local remedies, the use of insulting language and the abuse of right must lead to the conclusion that the Communication is inadmissible.

Concerning the exhaustion of local remedies, the Respondent State puts forward that it is premature for the Complainants to conclude that there were judicial delays. In support of such an argument, Cameroon dwells on the direct summons procedure relating to the use of the acronym and emblem "UPC" to note that the case was decided by the Court of Appeal on 21 November 2012. On the other hand, the Respondent State puts forward no argument as to the exhaustion of local remedies concerning the two other procedures. As to the use of disparaging or insulting language, the Respondent State likewise developed no argument.

Concerning the allegation of abuse of right, the Respondent State argues that it is proved by the Complainants' failure to establish a link between the numerous provisions of the Charter allegedly violated and the account of the facts. On this point, the State concludes that the Commission must sanction this lack of proof and correlation by declaring the Communication inadmissible.

The present Communication was submitted in accordance with Article 55 of the African Charter, which gives the Commission competence to receive and consider "communications other than those of States Parties". Such communications must, to be declared admissible, fulfil the requirements provided for in Article 56 of the African Charter.

In the present Communication, the Commission notes that the Parties agree on compliance with the admissibility requirements, with the exception of those laid down in paragraphs 3 and 5 of Article 56 of the African Charter. The Commission finds by itself that the Communication fulfils the other admissibility requirements. As regards the argument of the Respondent State based on an "abuse of right" attributable to the Complainants, the Commission will rule on it as a preliminary matter to the examination of the conformity of the Communication with the provisions whose observance is contested.

In support of its argument seeking a finding of an "abuse of right" on the part of the Complainants, the Respondent State puts forward the absence of a causal link between the facts denounced and the violations alleged. On this point, the Commission observes that it is now ruling on the admissibility of the Communication and that at this stage, it is content to determine the conformity of the application with the requirements laid down in Article 56 of the African Charter, in light of its jurisprudence. The subsequent examination is therefore limited to verifying compliance with procedural requirements on the basis of prima facie allegations of violations, without prejudice to the fact that the evidence of such violations will be provided by the Complainants at the merits stage. In any event, neither "abuse of right" nor the lack of proof of the violations can be retained in the examination of admissibility.

On the Respondent State's argument based on the use by the Communication of disparaging and insulting language, the Commission notes that Cameroon alleges the use of such language by the Complainants without, however, providing proof thereof, at any point in its brief in defence. Be that as it may, and in light of its consistent jurisprudence, the Commission notes that the Complainants did not use any language of this nature. Consequently, the Commission concludes that the Communication does comply with the provisions of Article 56(3) of the African Charter.

On the point of the Communication's compliance with the requirement of exhaustion of local remedies, the Commission will proceed to examine, one after the other, the three sets of proceedings in which the Complainants were involved before the courts of the Respondent State. The first proceeding is administrative and concerns the authorisation for the functioning of UPC-Manidem. Concerning the said proceeding, the Commission notes that Order No. 08/0/PCA/CS/93-94 of 13 December 1993 rendered by the Supreme Court of Cameroon, which declared unfounded the third-party opposition brought against the authorisation for the functioning of UPC-Manidem, put an end to the related administrative litigation. In the absence of any subsequent remedy and considering that the decisions of the Supreme Court cannot be appealed, the Commission concludes that local remedies have been exhausted, at least as regards the proceeding examined.

The second proceeding is civil and commercial, relating to the use of the acronym "UPC". With regard to this proceeding, the Commission notes that, the appellate court not having ruled on their counterclaim, the Complainants lodged an appeal on points of law before the Supreme Court of Cameroon, which took no action on their request. The Commission notes that at the time of its seizure in August 2012, the Complainants had still obtained no response whereas the decision of the Court of Appeal and the appeal before the Supreme Court date from 1998. In these circumstances, the Commission finds that the remedy was ineffective and that, by the benefit of the exception provided for in Article 56(5) of the African Charter, it is appropriate to conclude that the said remedy has been exhausted.

Finally, the Commission rules on the direct summons procedure concerning the use of the acronym and emblems of the "UPC". In this regard, the Commission notes that between 30 June 2011, the date on which the Complainants appealed against the decision of the first court, and the seizure of the Commission on 23 August 2012, a period of one year and two months had elapsed. It remains to be determined whether, as the Complainants allege, such a period is abnormally long. In light of its jurisprudence, among others in Modise v. Botswana and Association of Victims of Post Electoral Violence v. Cameroon, the Commission recalls that such an assessment must be made on a case-by-case basis, according to the circumstances of each case. In its above-cited precedents, the Commission ruled among other things on the basis of the situation of the Complainant, the domestic law of the Respondent State or the nature of the alleged violations.

On the factor related to the situation of the Complainant, the Commission notes that, even though they complain of harassment in the exercise of their activities, the judgment of the Supreme Court authorising the functioning of their political party guaranteed the Complainants the enjoyment of an intangible legal situation. As regards the nature of the alleged violations, the Commission notes that they are neither serious, nor of a nature to cause the Complainants serious and irreparable personal prejudice. Finally, as regards the factor related to the domestic law of the Respondent State, the Commission notes that Cameroonian law does not prescribe a time limit for the examination of an appeal in direct summons proceedings such as the one involving the Complainants.

In the present case, the Commission notes in particular that at the date of its seizure, the case had been called several times over a period of one year. In any event, criminal-type proceedings are generally of relative length since they require a more complex investigation. The Commission is of the view that, in such type of proceedings, a period of one year cannot be considered abnormally long unless it is justified that the Complainant is in an exceptionally critical situation or that the violations are of a certain gravity, which is not the case here. In these circumstances, the Commission concludes that the period of one year and two months was not abnormally long and that local remedies have not been exhausted with regard to the third proceeding.
In view of the foregoing, the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights declares the present Communication admissible in accordance with the provisions of Article 56 of the Charter.

The Complainants allege the violation of their rights to equality and equal protection of the law. In support of this allegation, they report the Respondent State's refusal to recognise the legal existence of their party, the UPC, while authorising the functioning of the UPC (KODOCK), which would be a dissident faction of it.

The Complainants further cite the State's refusal to respect the judgment of the Administrative Chamber of the Supreme Court authorising the functioning of the new party, UPC-Manidem, which they created in the hope of escaping the harassment that had made the peaceful functioning of the UPC impossible. This harassment allegedly took the form of a refusal of authorisation or a blocking by the police of all the activities of UPC-Manidem whereas those of the UPC (KODOCK) were authorised by the competent authority. Their counterclaim for annulment of the exclusivity of the acronym UPC in favour of the UPC (KODOCK) has remained without action before the Supreme Court since 1998.

The Complainants allege the failure to be tried within a reasonable time, the lack of impartiality and the absence of independence of the Cameroonian judicial system. Concerning reasonable time, they allege that the Supreme Court's failure to take any action on the counterclaim lodged in 1998 violates the provisions of Article 7(1)(d) of the Charter.

To prove the lack of impartiality, the Complainants report that the High Court of Wouri convicted the President of the UPC, Ndoh Michel, without having ruled on the possibility for an individual or group of individuals to protect the acronym and emblems of a political party. They argue that the lack of jurisdiction invoked is unfounded because the Court has full jurisdiction.

On the same ground, the Complainants argue that it is impartial for the Court of Appeal to annul the conviction of the lower court but refuse to rule on the nullity of the protection of the acronym and emblems of the UPC. In addition, the Complainants indicate that in the direct summons proceedings which were not declared admissible by the Commission, the Court of Douala-Bonanjo had given a follow-up similar to that of the Court of Wouri. They argue that such similarity proves the bias of the Cameroonian courts, which are instrumentalised by the executive power.

The Complainants argue that the order of the Supreme Court authorising the functioning of UPC-Manidem is rather due to the fact that, being a few months from his retirement, the President of the Administrative Chamber had been able to show a certain impartiality. The Complainants continue along the same lines to argue that the absence of independence of the judicial system is in itself a cause of partiality owing in particular to the fact that the President of the Republic, head of the executive power, is also guarantor of the independence of the judiciary, appoints the magistrates and chairs the Higher Judicial Council.

The Complainants argue that the gagging of the UPC prevents the members of the party from disseminating their ideas and opinions, thereby violating their rights protected under Article 9 of the Charter.

To support the allegation of violation of these provisions of the Charter, the Complainants invoke the numerous refusals to authorise meetings and the actual prevention by the police. They conclude that these acts violate their freedoms of association and assembly.

The Complainants allege that the refusal of authorisation to function, the refusal to execute court decisions and the various obstacles to holding their activities violate the right to participate freely in the government of their country.

In response to the Complainants' allegations on this point, the Respondent State argues that the assessment of equality can be made only in the presence of two identical situations. The State considers in this regard that there can be no question of discrimination when one considers the flourishing of political parties, of which at least 288 are authorised to operate freely in Cameroon.

Concerning the specific case of the UPC, the Respondent State reports that after the adoption of Law No. 1990/056 of 19 December 1990 this party applied for and obtained authorisation in the same way as many other political parties. The State nevertheless indicates that the Complainants never submitted an application for authorisation and that there is no political party called UPC-MANIDEM or UPC-KODOCK.

The Respondent State mentions, however, that in the wake of the above-cited Law liberalising political activity in Cameroon, dissensions within the UPC gave rise to several factions; that it is in the midst of these dissensions that the administration received in January 1991 an application for authorisation of the legal existence of the UPC party, to which a favourable response was given on 12 February 1991.

The State argues that such an authorisation then constituted an automatic bar to any other application concerning the same acronym and that, consequently, the application of UPC-MANIDEM had been rejected whereas an authorisation had been issued to the party called MANIDEM. Such a practice, according to the Respondent State, is well recognised by the Commission, which considers that a right may be limited for the needs of the organisation of the State.

As regards the Complainants' judicial disputes, the State rejects any implication, indicating that the administration never brought a lawsuit against the Complainants nor participated in any proceedings involving them. As for the prohibitions of meetings and the related police interventions, the State argues that they are well founded in that it cannot be possible to authorise the activities of a party that operates without legal authorisation.

The Respondent State concludes that the allegation of violation of the right to a fair trial is unfounded by referring to the decision rendered by the Littoral Court of Appeal in favour of the Complainants but also to that of the Administrative Chamber annulling that of the administration for abuse of power.

In response to the argument based on the absence of independence of the judiciary, the State argues that the fact that the President of the Republic is "guarantor of the Magistracy" in no way infringes such independence given that the judges of the bench are subject only to the law and their conscience.

According to the Respondent State, the Complainants being unable to prove the legal existence of an authorised political party, they cannot claim the enjoyment of any of the rights whose violation they allege.

Relative to political participation, the Respondent State argues that there was no violation of this right given that the Complainants did not meet the legal criterion for investiture by a political party authorised to participate in an election in Cameroon. The State further indicates that the UPC did participate in all electoral consultations in Cameroon since 1992.

Under Article 2 of the African Charter, every individual is entitled to the enjoyment of the rights guaranteed in the Charter without distinction of any kind, notably ... political or any other opinion ... or other status. As for Article 3, it stipulates that "1. Every individual shall be equal before the law. 2. Every individual shall be entitled to equal protection of the law". From the wording of these two provisions, it emerges that whereas Article 3 guarantees the right to equality, Article 2 defines the scope of this right by prescribing non-discrimination as the principal prohibition by which respect for the right to equality must be judged. In other words, Article 3 guarantees a right and Article 2 lays down a prohibition. When the two provisions are invoked concomitantly, as is the case here, the allegation of their violation must be examined jointly.

Discrimination is an unlawful or unjustified differentiation, that is, one based on one of the distinctions cited in Article 2 of the Charter, in this case political opinion, here alleged, or other status. As regards equal protection of the law, in Zimbabwe Lawyers for Human Rights and Another v. Zimbabwe, the Commission interprets it as the right recognised for every person to have equal access to the courts and to be treated equally by them both in procedures and in substance. It goes without saying that the Charter recognises as inherent in the right to equal protection of the law a tacit guarantee of non-discrimination in proceedings before the courts and in the application of the law to persons in an identical or similar situation.

This being so, as soon as the discrimination proscribed in Article 2 is constituted, there is necessarily a breach of the right to equality protected in Article 3. In the present Communication, the Commission will therefore examine the allegations of discrimination made by the Complainants in order to conclude whether or not there is a violation of Articles 2 and 3 depending on whether the discrimination is constituted or not.

The Commission agrees with the Respondent State that differentiation necessarily implies a comparator. However, this comparator could be explicit or implicit, known or presumed. In any event, as soon as the differentiation is based on political opinion or any other distinction, it is presumed unlawful until proven otherwise.

In the present case, it emerges from the arguments invoked by the Parties that Law No. 1990/056 of 19 December 1990 on the liberalisation of political life in Cameroon placed the Complainants in a position of equality with all the other citizens and leaders of political parties existing at the time. The grievances raised by the Complainants rather relate to the enjoyment of this equality in practice, the violation of which they argue by alleging a series of discriminations.

In this regard, the Commission notes that after the entry into force of the above-mentioned law, the two political parties in existence in Cameroon were that of the Complainants, the UPC, and the Cameroon People's Democratic Movement (CPDM). The Complainants then addressed to the administration in December 1990 a correspondence indicating the intention of the already existing UPC party to resume its activities in application of the provisions of the new law. However, they were met with a rejection for lack of legal existence. On the other hand, the administration had subsequently authorised to function a new political party also called UPC (however under the leadership of KODOCK and others) whose leaders submitted an application for authorisation only on 4 January 1991.

The Commission finds that in such a situation, the Complainants' UPC had at least two comparators, notably the CPDM and the UPC subsequently authorised by the administration, which will be identified here as UPC-KODOCK for ease of reference. With the CPDM, the Complainants' UPC, pre-existing the Law of 19 December 1990, had an identity of enjoyment of the implicit authorisation granted by the new law in the sense that there was no need for the Complainants to submit an application for authorisation, still less to obtain one, to carry out their activities.

In its brief on the merits, the Respondent State indeed cites the provisions of Article 21 of the said Law under which "political parties that exist legally at the date of promulgation of this law do not have to apply for a new authorisation". The State does not contest the existence of the Complainants' UPC at the reference date, namely that of the entry into force of the new law. The manifest conclusion is that the new law entailed authorisation to resume functioning and thus automatic legal existence of the Complainants' UPC from 19 December 1990. In these circumstances, two major legal situations had formed: that which prevailed at the liberalisation of the functioning of political parties in 1990 and that which prevailed thereafter.

In the first situation, the Commission notes that in its brief on the merits, the Respondent State indicates that several parties existing before and after independence applied for and obtained an authorisation, without however citing the parties pre-existing the adoption of the new law. Be that as it may, the Commission considers that the relevant provisions of the said law equate the tacit recognition of the parties pre-existing the entry into force of the law with the recognition by required authorisation of the parties created thereafter, notably the Cameroonian Socialist Union, the Cameroonian Democratic Party and even the UPC registered under the leadership of KODOCK and others cited by the State in its brief on the merits. It must therefore be noted that these political parties were valid comparators and that, by requiring the Complainants' UPC to obtain an authorisation already granted by the new law but by authorising the said comparators in an identical situation, the Respondent State applied a different treatment. For discrimination to be constituted, it would in addition have to be unjustified.

On the justification of the difference in treatment, the Respondent State alleges the vigour of Cameroonian democracy proved by the existence of 288 political parties authorised to function. In addition, the State argues that, having already issued an authorisation to function to the UPC (KODOCK) on 12 February 1991, there was a legal impediment to the issuance of a subsequent authorisation to the UPC (MANIDEM).

Concerning the number of political parties authorised to function in Cameroon, the Commission notes that it cannot in any way justify the difference in treatment to which the Complainants' party was subjected. As for the legal impediment put forward by the Respondent State, the Commission considers that the date of authorisation of 12 February 1991 indicated by the State is well after that of 19 December 1990 on which the Complainants' UPC obtained full legality to function without the need for any express authorisation from the administration. The State does not contest this established fact and does not provide proof to the contrary that its administration rejected the Complainants' letter of information on grounds of lack of legal existence. On the finding of the absence of justification for the difference in treatment, the Commission concludes that discrimination is constituted concerning the legal situation prevailing before the entry into force of Law No. 1990/056 of 19 December 1990.

The second situation is that which prevailed after the adoption of the new law and which required an express authorisation to operate as a political party in Cameroon. The Commission notes that the Respondent State, having already granted an authorisation to the KODOCK wing of the UPC, decided, by letter of 22 September 1992, to reject the Complainants' application to carry out political activities under the aegis of a party called UPC-MANIDEM for double use of the acronym UPC. Seized by the Complainants, the Supreme Court had then, by order dated 16 December 1992, annulled the said letter, thus enshrining the legal existence of the party UPC-MANIDEM.

However, the authorities of the Respondent State have, by various means, hindered the functioning of the party UPC-MANIDEM authorised by the Supreme Court. It emerges from the information contained in the file that despite the decision of the Supreme Court of 16 December 1992, the security forces of the Respondent State intervened through arrests, sequestrations and other forms of harassment to prevent meetings of UPC-MANIDEM organised in August 1995, August 2008, August 2011, February 2013 and August 2014.

The State does not contest the veracity of the refusals to authorise meetings and the police interventions. To justify the various impediments thus mentioned, the Respondent State alleges the lack of legal existence of the UPC (MANIDEM) for double use of the acronym UPC. In this regard, the Commission notes that the decision of the Supreme Court dating from 1992 and recalled above establishes the legality of the UPC (MANIDEM). While it is true that an action was brought in court against the double use of the acronym UPC, the appeal on points of law lodged in this regard by the Complainants before the Supreme Court against the decisions of the courts of first instance and appeal has remained without action since 1998. The decisions of the Supreme Court being final, they have the force of res judicata until the same court rules on a new application concerning the same case. It goes without saying that the order of the highest court authorising the functioning of the UPC (MANIDEM) remains valid. This validity defeats the Respondent State's argument based on the lack of legal existence of the UPC (MANIDEM).

In these circumstances, it remains to be determined to what extent the acts of the administration reported above were discriminatory and how equality was broken. On this point, the Commission refers to the Respondent State's brief on the merits, in which it clearly indicates that subsequent to the adoption of Law No. 1990/056, several political parties such as the Cameroonian Social Union (USC), the Cameroon People's Party (CPP) and the Cameroonian Democratic Party (PDC) obtained an authorisation and freely conduct their activities. It follows that the impediments to which the UPC (MANIDEM) was subjected are unjustified and constitute discrimination. There was therefore a breach of the right to equal protection of the law, in this case because the security forces of the Respondent State should have guaranteed the Complainants the same right to hold their meetings and other activities as is the case for all the other political parties cited by the Respondent State. The Commission concludes that the provisions of Articles 2 and 3 of the Charter have been violated.

Under the provisions of Article 7(1)(d), every individual has the right to be tried within a reasonable time by an impartial court. In its jurisprudence on the reasonable time of administration of justice, the Commission carries out an assessment on a case-by-case basis, notably on the basis of factors such as the facts of the case, the situation of the Complainant and the domestic law of the Respondent State. In any event, it is in light of the circumstances of the case and the complexity of the issues brought before the courts that the reasonable or unreasonable nature of the time of administration of justice should be determined.

In the present case, the Parties agree that, in the case of UPC (KODOCK) against the Complainants tried at first instance by the High Court of Wouri, the appellate judge rendered a decision but that the appeal on points of law lodged before the Supreme Court of Cameroon in 1998 had not been followed up as of the date of the present examination. The Commission notes that the main issue in dispute before the domestic courts is that of the Complainants' right to participate in the political life of their country. On a question of such great importance, and considering that the appeal before the Supreme Court concerned the mere refusal of the Court of Appeal to rule on a counterclaim, the Commission considers that a period of 18 years is not reasonable.

On the argument based on the lack of impartiality of the domestic courts, the Commission is of the view, with the European Court of Human Rights when it considers in Cubber v. Belgium that the impartiality of judges is the fundamental condition of the "confidence which the courts must inspire in the courts in a democratic society". The Commission notes that as such impartiality stems mainly from the impression that the judicial system gives to the litigant and therefore from a logic relating mainly to appearances. Given the subtle nature of its expression, it is therefore in light of the theory of appearances that the jurisprudence assesses impartiality.

In its relevant jurisprudence, the European Court distinguishes a twofold impartiality: subjective of the judge and objective of the court. In Remli v. France, for example, the Court considers, concerning the subjective approach, that the personal conviction of a given judge on a given occasion must be sought. In that case, the applicant of Maghrebi origin had lodged a request for legitimate suspicion after one of the assize jurors declared, outside the hearing, "what is more, I am racist". The Court had then held that the Assize Court's failure to take this legitimate suspicion into account in the composition of the assize jury left the legitimacy of the suspicion of the Court's partiality standing. To assess the subjective impartiality of the assize judges, the Court considers as a determining element "whether the applicant's apprehensions can be regarded as objectively justified" and that there is a duty for the court concerned to examine any challenge arising as to its impartiality insofar as such a challenge is serious.

As for the objective approach, it consists in establishing that other functions of a judge are likely to give rise to a prejudgment of partiality or the appearance of partiality. For example, in the above-cited Cubber case, the Court condemns the fact that a prosecution magistrate may sit in a trial court. In Mancel and Branquart, it concludes that the Court of Cassation, which had already ruled on a first appeal, was biased. On the basis of the "theory of appearances" adopted in Piersack v. Belgium, the Court places the burden of proof on the applicant given that the presumption of partiality is only rebuttable. In sum, the judge must be free of any prejudice. The necessity of such an absence of prejudice shows clearly from the position of the European Court when it says in M v. France that it suffices to note that "... the impartiality of the Court of Cassation could give rise to serious doubts and that the applicant's fears could be regarded as objectively justified".

In the present case, as regards subjective impartiality, the Complainant puts forward the fact that different courts reached the same conclusion - erroneous in his understanding - on the same question. In this regard, the Commission notes that on the same dispute concerning the validity of the protection of the acronym and emblems of the UPC (KODOCK), the High Court of Wouri, the Littoral Court of Appeal and the Court of First Instance of Douala-Bonanjo reached the same decision to reject his counterclaim for annulment of the acronym and emblems of the UPC (KODOKC), apparently for lack of capacity.

The Commission notes that such lack of capacity is only apparent since in reality, instead of a rejection for lack of capacity, it was a matter of a lack of reasoning and a denial of justice. As proof, the relevant grounds of the decision of the High Court of Wouri read "whereas the grounds put forward in support of this (counter)claim prove unfounded; whereas it is therefore appropriate to dismiss the defendant party from this claim". The Commission notes that this reasoning not revealing a lack of jurisdiction, the court did not rule on its jurisdiction, still less did it give reasons for the lack of foundation of the Complainants' claim. In addition, the State does not contest the Complainants' allegation that the High Court, which enjoys full jurisdiction, cannot use as a pretext a material incapacity to refuse to rule on the counterclaim concerning the nullity of the protection of the acronym UPC.

With regard to the Court of Appeal, the Commission notes that it considered that it could not "examine the other grounds without having examined the question of incapacity". Consequently, the Court concluded as to the jurisdiction of the first judge only on the amount of the claim, which had been raised, by oral submissions, from the three million CFA francs requested in the originating application to 350 million, that is beyond the legal limit of 5 million. The Court's decision to overturn the judgment appealed against therefore drew its ground only from this sole failure to respect the subject-matter jurisdiction of the lower court judge. In addition, the Commission notes that, having annulled the conviction by the High Court of one of the Complainants, Mr Michel NDOH, the Court of Appeal nevertheless refused to rule on the nullity of the protection of the acronym UPC, the use of which was nevertheless the main ground of the said conviction. The appellate judge had, in any event, dispensed with all the other grounds raised by the parties.

It can easily be concluded that the two courts simply omitted or refused to rule on the counterclaim lodged by the Complainants. In addition, the fact that a third court, in this case the Court of First Instance of Doula-Bonanjo, adopted the same position in the same dispute otherwise brought may form the basis of a legitimate suspicion of prejudgment, bias and therefore of absence of impartiality. The arguments put forward by the Complainants in this regard were duly recalled above.

The Commission considers that, given the complex nature of impartiality, which is difficult to prove, notably subjective impartiality, appearances constitute the most reliable recourse since one cannot materially probe the inner motivations of the judge, notably his intimate conviction. In particular, in constitutional democracies governed by the separation of powers, the independence of the judge should be assessed in light of the adage "justice must not only be done, it must also be seen to be done". The European Court of Human Rights agrees when it concludes in Konstas v. Greece for example, that public statements by members of the government, mainly the minister of justice, necessarily give the public the impression that there is interference with the course of justice. The guarantee of impartiality must consequently necessarily be assessed in light of the independence of the judicial system, notably vis-à-vis the executive and legislative powers.

Relative to this independence of the courts, the Commission concluded, in the Meldrum v. Zimbabwe case, that it necessarily presupposes the absence of pressure or interference. In the same logic, when examining the Wetsh'okonda Koso and Others v. Democratic Republic of Congo case, the Commission considered that the independence of the courts must in any event be assessed with regard to the executive power. As factors of assessment, the Commission retained, among others, appointment, security of tenure, protection against external pressures and the perception of independence. In addition, and very notably, the Commission concluded that there was an absence of independence of the judiciary in Gunme and Others v. Cameroon on the finding that the Higher Judicial Council was chaired by the President of the Republic assisted by the Minister of Justice.

Likewise, the European Court of Human Rights holds, notably in the leading decisions Medvedyev v. France and Moulin v. France, that the public prosecutor is disqualified from exercising judicial functions notably for lack of independence vis-à-vis the executive power.

In the present case, the Commission notes that whereas the Constitution of the Respondent State establishes the separation of powers as a central pillar of the rule of law, the provisions of Article 37(3) of the same Constitution invest the President of the Republic as the guarantor of the independence of the judiciary. In addition, the President of the Republic is also the President of the Higher Judicial Council, the body in charge of the appointment of magistrates, the management of their careers and the functioning of the judicial system.

Moreover, turning to other elements of legitimate suspicion that were not contested by the Respondent State, the Commission notes that the Complainants put forward that "the judges themselves, outside of court, declared themselves sorry to have rendered decisions against the law and their conscience, in order to comply with the injunctions of the government and openly complain of the absence of independence of the judicial system in Cameroon".

In such a system where one power intervenes so directly and decisively in the functioning of another power, the legitimate suspicion is well founded by the theory of appearances examined above. In the present case, it is established that the Complainants' UPC has always been a party historically opposed to the ruling party which largely controls the executive power. The Commission also noted that, in their multiple attempts to peacefully carry out their political activities as UPC or UPC-MANIDEM, the Complainants suffered numerous setbacks despite the decisions rendered in their favour by the domestic courts, including the Supreme Court.

In response to the allegation of partiality, the Respondent State argues that the fact that the administrative judge rendered a decision in favour of the Complainants well attests to the absence of interference by the executive power in the functioning of the courts. The Commission notes that this decision mentioned by the Respondent State cannot by itself suffice to demonstrate the impartiality of the courts. As the facts attest, the judge concerned was a few months from his retirement, which is likely to justify the freedom of mind that characterised the impartiality of his positions. Moreover, as examined above, impartiality can be both subjective, targeting a single judge, or objective, targeting the whole court ruling on the case, several courts or even the whole judicial system as the case may be. By the benefit of all these grounds, the Commission concludes that the provisions of Article 7(1)(d) of the Charter have been violated.

The provisions whose violation is alleged guarantee the rights to the dissemination of one's opinions, to assembly, to association and to political participation. The State argues that the lack of legal authorisation to function of their political party renders the Complainants unfit for the enjoyment of the rights thus guaranteed.

The Commission considers that, in view of the Complainants' claims, the rights whose violation is alleged are inherent in the functioning of a political party. It is therefore appropriate to rule on them jointly, by examining first the allegation of violation of the right to political participation.

The right to political participation is protected by the provisions of Article 13(1) of the Charter, which guarantee the rights to elect and to be elected in accordance with the law. As the Respondent State indicates in its brief on the merits, the benefit of these rights is effective in Cameroon only within the framework of authorised political parties so that an authorisation entails enjoyment of the rights concerned.

In examining the essential components of the right to political participation, the Commission decided in Mamboundou v. Gabon that it includes, among other things, transparency in the participation of candidates and political parties in animating political life and in elections. In addition, in the case of Constitutional Rights Project and Civil Liberties Organisation v. Nigeria the Commission considered that the right to political participation: "... implies, among other things, the right to vote for the representative of one's choice (...) and that the annulment of the results constitutes a violation of this right". Finally, in its decision Lawyers for Human Rights v. Swaziland it concluded that "the adoption of a law prohibiting the creation of political parties seriously undermines the capacity of citizens to participate in the conduct of the affairs of their country, in violation of Article 13 of the Charter".

In light of these precedents, the Commission notes that the assessment of the free nature of political participation should be made in light of factors linked to the conduct of the Respondent State in the face of citizens' initiatives aimed at the enjoyment of this right. In this case, since such enjoyment is subject to compliance with the law, it will be a matter of determining whether citizens enjoyed free access once they had complied with it.

In the present case, the Commission finds that the Complainants' UPC, pre-existing the new law, was prevented from functioning. In addition, the UPC-MANIDEM subsequently authorised by the Supreme Court was the subject of constant harassment violating the authority of the order of the highest court. The unreasonable length of the proceedings aimed at restoring such authority completed the crystallisation of the violation. The arguments developed on the violation of the right to equality are applicable with regard to the right to political participation. By the benefit of these arguments, the Commission concludes that the provisions of Article 13(1) have been violated.

On the right to the dissemination of one's opinions, the Commission notes that it constitutes the very essence of the creation of a political party whose aim is to win power by disseminating its political ideas, opinions and programme among the electorate. As for the freedoms of assembly and association, they constitute the guarantee that makes the dissemination of political opinions possible. When political parties cannot meet freely or citizens cannot freely form political parties, the right to disseminate their political opinions is mortgaged. These violations being subsequent to that of the right to political participation, it must be concluded that Articles 9, 10 and 11 of the Charter have been violated.

The Commission having received the Complainants' arguments, it is appropriate to examine the related claims. Where, as is the case here, the Complainant does not produce the specific scales for determining the damages requested, the Commission has discretion to quantify the reparation or refer to the domestic bodies of the Respondent State. In any event, reparation must be just, adequate, effective, sufficient, appropriate, victim-oriented and proportionate to the prejudice suffered.

On the full reinstatement of the UPC created in 1948, the Commission notes that it could be technically complex to grant it given that the name UPC has already been attributed to another political group which has made full use of it over time. The main object of the Complaint being the enjoyment of the right to political participation, the Commission considers that the authorisation to exercise this right under the name UPC MANIDEM is capable of providing for it. It goes without saying that the Complainants must be able to enjoy their full civil and political rights, in this case that of political participation under the banner of the political formation they created and which is legal under the law in force.

As for compensation for prejudice, the facts of the case sufficiently prove that significant prejudice was caused to the Complainants. It is appropriate to require reparation for it. The Commission, For these reasons,
Finds that the Republic of Cameroon has violated the provisions of Articles 2, 3, 7(1)(d), 9, 10, 11, 13 and 26 of the Charter. Consequently:

Noting the important role played by the police in ensuring the peaceful conduct of public assemblies and consequently, protecting freedom of expression and assembly;
Mindful of the importance of communication and the right of access to information before, during and after assemblies;

Concerned by the persistence of police violence during assemblies in Africa and its apparent consequences on the enjoyment of the various rights enshrined in the African Charter, in particular Articles 4, 5, 6, 9 and 11;
Considering the particularly vulnerable state of human rights defenders and journalists who are more exposed to various forms of police violence during assemblies;

ANNEX - CRITERIA FOR THE GRANTING OF AND FOR MAINTAINING OBSERVER STATUS WITH THE AFRICAN COMMISSION ON HUMAN AND PEOPLES’ RIGHTS
CHAPTER I

1. All Non-Governmental Organisations (NGOs) applying for observer status with the African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights (the Commission) shall be expected to submit a documented application to the Secretariat of the Commission, with a view to showing their willingness and capability to work for the realisation of the objectives of the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights (the African Charter).
2. All NGOs applying for observer status with the Commission shall consequently:

a) Have objectives and activities in consonance with the fundamental principles and objectives enunciated in the African Union (AU) Constitutive Act, the preamble to the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights, and the Protocol to the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights on the Rights of Women in Africa (the Maputo Protocol);
b) Be NGOs working in the field of human rights in Africa; and
c) Declare their financial resources.
3. NGOs applying for Observer Status with the Commission are required to provide, at least three months prior to the Ordinary Session, the following documents:
a) A letter of application addressed to the Secretariat requesting Observer Status with the Commission;
b) A list of the Board of Members, and other members of the NGO;
c) The signed and authenticated Constitutive Statute of the NGO;
d) The Certificate of Legal Status of the NGO issued by the relevant Government authority, in the country in which the NGO is based;
e) The sources of funding of the NGO;
f) The latest independently audited financial statement of the NGO;
g) The latest Annual Activity Report of the NGO; and

h) A current comprehensive Plan of Action or Strategic Plan for the NGO, signed or approved by the relevant members of the NGO, which covers a minimum of two years, and which contains the objectives of the NGO during the specified period, the list of activities to be carried out, the timeline for their realisation, the places of implementation, the strategies to implement them and the target groups.”
4. No application for Observer Status shall be put forward for examination by the Commission without having been previously processed by the Secretariat.
5. The Commission’s Bureau shall designate a rapporteur to examine the dossiers. The Commission’s decision shall be notified without delay to the applicant NGO.
CHAPTER II: PARTICIPATION OF NGOS WITH OBSERVER STATUS IN PROCEEDINGS OF THE COMMISSION
1. a) All NGOs with Observer Status (observers) shall be invited to be present at the opening and closing sessions of the Commission.
b) An observer shall not participate in the Commission’s proceedings in any manner other than as provided for in the Rules of Procedure governing the conduct of its sessions.
2. All observers shall have access to the documents of the Commission subject to the condition that such documents:
a) shall not be of a confidential nature;

b) deal with issues that are of relevance to their interests. The distribution of general information documents shall be free of charge; the distribution of specialised documents shall be on a paid-for basis, except where reciprocal arrangements are in place.
3. Observers may be invited specially to be present at closed sessions dealing with issues of particular interest to them.

4. Observers may be authorised by the Chairperson of the Commission to make a statement on an issue that concerns them, subject to the text of the statement having been provided, with sufficient lead-time, to the Chairperson of the Commission through the Secretary to the Commission.
5. The Chairperson of the Commission may give the floor to observers to respond to questions directed at them by participants.

6. Observers may request to have issues of a particular interest to them included in the provisional agenda of the Commission, in accordance with the provisions of the Rules of Procedure of the Commission.
CHAPTER III: RELATIONS BETWEEN THE COMMISSION AND OBSERVERS
1. Observers shall undertake to establish close relations of co-operation with the Commission and to engage in regular consultations with it on matters of common interest.
2. Observers shall present their activity reports to the Commission every two years.
3. Administrative arrangements shall be made, whenever necessary, to determine the modalities of this co-operation.
CHAPTER IV: FINAL PROVISIONS

1. The provisions of the General Convention on the Privileges and Immunities of the OAU and those of the Headquarters Agreement of the Commission shall not apply to observers except as regards the granting of visas.
2. The Commission reserves the right to take the following measures against Observers that are in default of their obligations:
- non-participation in sessions;
- denial of documents and information;
- denial of the opportunity to propose items to be included in the Commission’s provisional agenda and of participating in its proceedings.
3. Observer status may be suspended or withdrawn from any NGO that does not fulfil the present criteria, after deliberation by the Commission.

The African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights (the Commission) meeting at its 59 th Ordinary Session from 21 October to 4 November 2016 in Banjul, Islamic Republic of The Gambia;
Recalling its mandate to promote and protect human and peoples’ rights pursuant to the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights (the African Charter);
Bearing in mind that the Islamic Republic of the Gambia is a State Party to the African Charter and a signatory to the African Charter on Democracy, Elections and Governance;

Recalling the Guidelines and Measures for the Prohibition and Prevention of Torture, Cruel, Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment in Africa; Guidelines on the Conditions of Arrest, Police Custody and Pre-Trial Detention in Africa; Declaration of Principles on Freedom of Expression in Africa; Principles and Guidelines on the Right to a Fair Trial and Legal Assistance in Africa; and General Comment No. 3 on the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights on the Right to Life;

Further recalling its resolutions ACHPR/Res.5 (XI) 92 on the Right to Freedom of Association; ACHPR/Res.281 (LV) 14 on the Right to Peaceful Demonstration; and ACHPR/Res.331 (XIX) 16 on Elections in Africa;

Bearing in mind the Declaration of Principles of Freedom of Expression in Africa Principles I (2) which provides that “everyone shall have an equal opportunity to exercise the right to freedom of expression and to access information without discrimination” and Principle II (2) which also provides that “any restrictions on freedom of expression shall be provided by law, serve a legitimate interest and be necessary in a democratic society”;

Reaffirming the fundamental importance of freedom of information, expression and association of individuals as a cornerstone of democracy, particularly during elections and, as a means of ensuring respect for all human rights and freedoms;
Concerned by the three-year imprisonment of opposition party members for protesting against election reforms introduced by the Election Amendment Act of 2015;

Alarmed by the deaths of Ebrima Solo Sandeng on 15 May 2016 and Ebrima Solo Krummah on 20 August 2016, National Organising Secretary and Member of the United Democratic Party (UDP) respectively, following their arrest and detention by the police for demonstrating against these electoral reforms;
Deeply concerned by allegations of torture and ill-treatment of the detained opposition members as well as sexual assault of detained women;
Further concerned by the allegations that detained persons in need of medical care denied the medical attention and family visits;
Disturbed by Government restrictions on social media and certain sites of the internet;
The Commission:
1. Condemns all acts of excessive and disproportionate use of force against protestors, sexual assault of women detainees and torture and other ill-treatment of detainees;
2. Condemns unjustified restrictions on the right of freedom of expression and access to the internet by the Government;
3. Calls on the Government of Islamic Republic of The Gambia to:
a) Ensure that the elections are free, fair and peaceful;
b) Pardon all persons sentenced because of demonstrating to oppose election reforms of the Election Amendment Act;
c) Refrain from the use of excessive and disproportionate force against protestors and generally take necessary measures to ensure the security and safety of its population;
d) Release the report of the investigation into the death of Ebrima Solo Sandeng if it has been concluded;
e) Carry out prompt and impartial investigations into the death of Ebrima Solo Krummah while in detention and make public the report of the investigating body;

f) Carry out prompt and impartial investigations into the allegations of torture, ill-treatment and sexual assault of detainees and ensure that those responsible are held accountable and subjected to appropriate sanctions reflecting the gravity of the offences, in accordance with the relevant international and regional standards;
g) Ensure immediate provision of medical assistance for detainees and prisoners in need of it and allow visits by their families and legal representatives;
h) Immediately lift all restrictions to internet and social media networks it has imposed; and
i) Ensure that contesting parties and candidates of the elections are given equitable access to state controlled media.
4. Calls on leaders and members of opposition parties, other stakeholders and the general population to refrain from violence and maintain peace during and after the elections.

The African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights (the Commission), meeting at its 59 th Ordinary Session held from 21 October to 4 November 2016 in Banjul, Islamic Republic of The Gambia;

Bearing in mind the obligations of the Gabonese Republic as a State Party to the African Charter and other regional and international human rights instruments, and signatory tothe African Charter on Democracy, Elections and Governance;

Reaffirming the provisions of Articles 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 9, 11 and 13 of the African Charter which guarantee the right to equal protection of the law, the right to life, the right not to be subjected to torture and other ill-treatment, the right to personal liberty and protection from arbitrary arrest, the right to a fair trial, the right to receive information and to freedom of expression, the right of assembly, and the right to participate freely in government;

The African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights (the Commission), meeting at its 59 th Ordinary Session held from 21 October to 4 November 2016 in Banjul, The Gambia;
Recalling its mandate to promote and protect human and peoples' rights under the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights (the African Charter);

Mindful of its Statement of 3 May 2015, made at its 56th Ordinary Session held from 21 April to 7 May 2015 in Banjul, The Gambia, and its Resolution ACHPR/Res.309 ( ( EXT.OS/XVIII) on the human rights situation in Burundi;

Recalling the decision of the Peace and Security Council of the African Union (PSC) of 17 December 2015 stressing that "only a genuine and truly inclusive dialogue, based on the respect of the Arusha Agreement and the Constitution of Burundi, will allow the Burundian stakeholders to overcome the serious difficulties facing their country, as well as strengthen social cohesion, democracy and the rule of law";

Considering the conclusions and recommendations contained in the Commission's report following its fact-finding mission undertaken in Burundi in December 2015 at the request of the Peace and Security Council, and the report of the United Nations Independent Investigation Mission on Burundi (UNIIB);

Deeply concerned about the security and human rights situation in Burundi marked by continuous arrests and arbitrary detentions, targeted killings, extrajudicial executions, acts of torture and other forms of cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment, abductions and enforced disappearances, harassment and intimidation of journalists and media professionals, sexual violence, and other forms of serious human rights violations;
Concerned by the continuous political impasse and the lack of constructive dialogue between all the stakeholders towards finding a peaceful solution to the crisis;

Further concerned by the decision of the Burundian authorities of 19 and 24 October 2016, to deregister five civil society organisations notably the Forum for the Strengthening of Civil Society (FORSC), Forum for Consciousness and Development (FOCODE), Association for the Protection of Human Rights and Detained Persons (APRODH), Action by Christians for the Abolition of Torture in Burundi (ACAT-Burundi) and Network of Honest Citizens (RCP); and to suspend five other organisations, including Civil Society Coalition for Election Monitoring (COSOME), Burundian Coalition for the International Criminal Court (CB-CPI), Burundi Union of Journalists (UBJ), Burundian Human Rights League “ ITEKA”, and SOS Torture Burundi; accused of conducting activities that are likely to disturb public order and security;

Concerned about the decision taken by the Burundian authorities to suspend cooperation with the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights in Burundi (HCHR) and to declare the UNIIB experts persona non grata, following the presentation of the final report of the Investigation Mission during the 33 rd Session of the UN Human Rights Council on 27 September 2016;
The Commission:
Condemns the various human rights violations committed in the country since April 2015;

Condemns the continuous repression against human rights defenders which led to the deregistration and suspension of the main human rights organisations and the suspension of independent media outlets in the country;
Regrets the decision of the Burundian authorities to suspend cooperation with the Office of the HCHR in Burundi and to declare the UNIIB experts persona non grata ;
Calls on the Government of the Republic of Burundi to:
i. immediately end all human rights violations;
ii. release all persons arbitrarily detained, especially persons detained incommunicado, and ensure their physical integrity;
iii. end attacks, threats, acts of intimidation and harassment, including judicial harassment, of human rights defenders and journalists;
iv. authorise the unconditional resumption of the activities of all the deregistered and suspended civil society organisations;
v. take the necessary urgent measures to conduct prompt, independent, impartial and effective investigations in order to prosecute the perpetrators of these crimes;

vi. ensure that victims of the above violations and their families obtain full and adequate redress, including restitution, compensation, rehabilitation, satisfaction and guarantees of non-repetition;

vii. extend full cooperation with all regional and international human rights institutions, including the Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights and the African Union particularly regarding the full deployment of all the human rights observers and military experts, in accordance with the decision of the Heads of State and Government of the African Union adopted at the 26 th Summit held from 21 to 31 January 2016;
viii. authorise the Commission to undertake a mission to follow up on the recommendations in the Report of the Fact-finding Mission;

The African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights (the Commission), meeting at its 59 th Ordinary Session held from 21 October to 4 November 2016 in Banjul, Islamic Republic of the Gambia;

Mindful of the obligations of the Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia as a Member State of the African Union, and State Party to the African Charter and the African Charter on Democracy, Elections and Governance as well as other regional human rights instruments;

Recalling that one of the objectives of the African Union is to promote and protect human and peoples’ rights in accordance with the African Charter, and to promote democratic principles and institutions, popular participation and good governance;

lift the ban on movement, assembly, media access, and internet services;

ensure due process of law for persons arrested and detained in connection with protests, in accordance with regional and international standards, and release persons arrested and detained without charge;
refrain from the use of excessive and disproportionate force against protestors and, more generally, take the necessary measures to guarantee the security and safety of its population;

initiate prompt and impartial investigations into these alleged human rights violations and ensure that the perpetrators of these violations are held accountable and subjected to appropriate sanctions reflecting the gravity of the offences, in accordance with relevant international and regional standards;

comply with the letter and spirit of the African Charter and other regional and international human rights instruments to which it is a party and, more particularly, the instruments referred to in this Resolution;

ensure that victims of the above violations and their families obtain full and adequate redress, including restitution, compensation, rehabilitation, satisfaction and guarantees of non-repetition; and
authorise the Commission to undertake a fact-finding mission to Ethiopia.

The African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights, meeting at its 20th Extra-Ordinary Session, held in Banjul, Islamic Republic of The Gambia, from 09 to 18 June 2016;
Recalling its mandate to promote and ensure the protection of human and peoples’ rights in Africa under the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights (the African Charter);

Bearing in mind Article 2 of the African Charter which guarantees every individual the enjoyment of the rights and freedoms recognized in the African Charter regardless of race, ethnic group, color, sex, language, religion, political or any other opinion, national and social origin, fortune, birth or other status;

Further bearing in mind Article 18(4) of the African Charter which provides that the persons with disabilities shall also have the right to special measures of protection in keeping with their physical or moral needs, in addition to Article 23 of the Protocol to the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights on the Rights of Women in Africa which provides for the special protection of women with disabilities;
Recalling Resolution ACHPR/Res.263 (LIV) 2013 on the prevention of attacks and discrimination against Persons with Albinism;

Further recalling the Joint Press Release by the Chairpersons of the Working Group on Death Penalty, Extra-Judicial, Summary and Arbitrary Killings in Africa and the Working Group on the Rights of Older Persons and Persons with Disabilities in Africa regarding the attacks and killings of Persons with Albinism in East Africa, issued on 11 March 2015;
Cognizant of the commemoration of the International Albinism Awareness Day on 13 June 2016;
Concerned at the widespread violence, discrimination, stigma and social exclusion directed at persons with albinism;
Deeply concerned about continuing systematic attacks and killings against persons with albinism in the Republic of Malawi;
Taking note of the commitment of the Government of the Republic of Malawi to fight this serious violation of the rights to life, dignity and protection from inhuman treatment;
The Commission:
(i) Strongly condemns the continuing systematic attacks and killings of persons with albinism;
(ii) Calls on the Republic of Malawi to urgently take all necessary measures to ensure the effective protection of persons with albinism and members of their families;

(iii) Calls on the Republic of Malawi to ensure accountability by duly investigating and bringing perpetrators of these gross human rights violations to justice, and by ensuring that victims and members of their families have access to appropriate remedies;
